items.title: Scope down permissions of existing sessions using AWS STS GetScopedCredentials
items.summary: When you build AI agents, you often want each agent or sub-agent to have only the permissions its tasks require, rather than the full permissions of the session that started it. GetScopedCredentials is a new AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) API that you can use to scope down the permissions of existing temporary security credentials. You can assign each agent, sub-agent, or process its own set of credentials that keep the caller’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity but carry reduced permissions, a shorter session duration, or both. You can call GetScopedCredentials with the temporary security credentials you already use, such as those from aws login, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance profile, or an AWS Lambda function. In each call, you pass a scope down policy, a shorter session duration, or both. A scope down policy is an inline policy that describes the maximum permissions for the new credentials. The resulting permissions are the intersection of your session’s effective permissions and the scope down policy, so they can only be reduced. Similarly, the session duration you request can’t exceed the remaining duration of the calling session. You can also call GetScopedCredentials again with the resulting credentials to scope down permissions or reduce session duration even further. GetScopedCredentials is designed as a building block. Because it scopes down permissions on the credentials you already have, you can build it into agent frameworks, services that issue credentials to other components, continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, and your own applications. You can also call it again with scoped-down credentials, so an orchestrating agent can give each sub-agent narrower access than its own. In this post, we walk through a few common use cases to get you started, show you how to call GetScopedCredentials, and explain how to manage access to it. Example use cases You can use GetScopedCredentials whenever a workload needs narrower access than the session that starts it. Examples include limiting what AI agents can do, scoping down permissions based on runtime context, and granting just-in-time access. We cover two of the most common use cases in more detail in this section. Limit what AI agents can do When you pass credentials to an agent, the agent can use any permission those credentials carry. An agent decides which actions to take at runtime, often based on prompts or tool output. If its credentials are overly permissive, an agent that makes a mistake can act beyond the task you gave it. Before you pass credentials to an agent, you can use GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions to only what its tasks require, such as read access to a single Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket. You could also take the opposite approach and keep most of its permissions while removing only the actions the agent should never perform, such as deleting resources. An orchestrating agent can do the same for each sub-agent it starts. Because a scope down operation can only narrow permissions, a sub-agent never has more access than the agent that started it. To help ensure that your agents only have access to the scoped-down credentials, run them in isolated or sandbox environments such as AWS Strands Box . Scope down permissions based on runtime context Many workloads run under a single IAM role but need different, narrower permissions for each task they perform. The right set of permissions for a task often depends on information the workload learns only at runtime, such as who sent a request. Consider a multi-tenant application that stores each tenant’s files under a separate prefix in one S3 bucket. This application uses a single IAM role to serve all its tenants, so the role can access every tenant’s prefix. However, each request should reach only the files of the tenant who sent it, and the application learns which tenant that is only after it authenticates the request. At that point, a trusted credential broker in the application takes the tenant details from the authenticated session and calls GetScopedCredentials with a scope down policy that allows access only to that tenant’s prefix. It passes only the scoped-down credentials to the worker that handles the request, so Amazon S3 denies that worker access to other tenants’ prefixes even though the original role covers them all. How to call GetScopedCredentials This section walks through the process of scoping down permissions for an existing session. Before you call GetScopedCredentials, make sure you have valid temporary security credentials and that they have the permissions to call the API. The following identity based policy grants that permission. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "sts:GetScopedCredentials", "Resource": "*" }] } To call GetScopedCredentials, use the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDK for your programming language. Step 1: Define a scope down policy Write a scope down policy that describes the maximum permissions the resulting credentials should have. At launch, GetScopedCredentials accepts one inline scope down policy of up to 2,048 characters. You can write a scope down policy in many ways, such as authoring a policy from scratch, reusing or modifying an existing policy, or asking an AI assistant to draft one. This section covers two such approaches. Option A: Write the policy yourself If you know which actions and resources your task needs, write the policy directly. The following sample policy allows the resulting credentials to only read objects from a single S3 bucket. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*" }] } Make sure to include every action the task needs, including dependent actions. For example, if your task uses Amazon Athena to query data in Amazon S3, the policy must also allow s3:GetObject on that data, because Athena reads it with your credentials. To keep most of the calling session’s permissions and remove only a few sensitive ones, use an Allow statement with NotAction . This statement doesn’t grant additional access, because a scope down policy can only reduce permissions. The resulting credentials keep the calling session’s permissions except the actions you list, which makes this a quick way to set guardrails without listing each action a task needs. The following sample policy blocks identity and account management, assuming other roles, and deleting some critical resources. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "NotAction": [ "iam:*", "organizations:*", "account:*", "sts:AssumeRole*", "s3:DeleteBucket", "ec2:TerminateInstances", "rds:DeleteDBInstance", "dynamodb:DeleteTable" ], "Resource": "*" }] } Option B: Generate the policy with IAM Policy Autopilot You can also use IAM Policy Autopilot to generate a scope down policy. IAM Policy Autopilot is an open source tool from AWS that analyzes the AWS SDK calls in your code and identifies the permissions it requires to run successfully. You can run it from the command line or as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in your AI coding assistant. To install it, see the Getting Started instructions for IAM Policy Autopilot. We’ll use the following Python code to generate a scope down policy using IAM Policy Autopilot. It records a report’s status in an Amazon DynamoDB table. import json import logging import os import boto3 from botocore.exceptions import ClientError logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) dynamodb = boto3.client("dynamodb") table_name = os.environ["TABLE_NAME"] def _response(status_code, message): return {"statusCode": status_code, "body": json.dumps({"message": message})} def handler(event, context): try: request = json.loads(event.get("body") or "{}") report_id = request["reportId"] except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, TypeError): return _response(400, "Request body must be JSON with a reportId") if not isinstance(report_id, str) or not report_id: return _response(400, "reportId must be a non-empty string") try: dynamodb.put_item( TableName=table_name, Item={ "reportId": {"S": report_id}, "status": {"S": "READY"}, }, ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(reportId)", ) return _response(200, "Report status saved") except ClientError as error: code = error.response["Error"]["Code"] if code == "ConditionalCheckFailedException": return _response(409, "Report status already exists") logger.error("PutItem failed: %s", code) return _response(500, "Unable to save the report status") Save the code as report_status.py and run the following command. If the generated policy exceeds the 2,048 character limit, set the max-policy-size and allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size options to 2048. IAM Policy Autopilot then replaces groups of actions with wildcards to fit that size and warns you if it can’t. iam-policy-autopilot generate-policies ./report_status.py \ --region us-west-2 \ --account 123456789012 \ --service-hints dynamodb \ --max-policy-size 2048 \ --allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size 2048 \ --pretty IAM Policy Autopilot returns the following policy. { "Id": "IamPolicyAutopilot", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:WriteDataForReplication" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-west-2:123456789012:table/*" ] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "kms:Decrypt" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/*" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": [ "dynamodb.us-west-2.amazonaws.com" ] } } } ] } IAM Policy Autopilot generates a starting policy that can include wildcards, either because specific resources can’t be inferred from the code, such as with the table/* and key/* resources in this example, or because an optional parameter that limits policy size replaced actions with wildcards. Review the generated policies and replace the wildcards with the actions and resources your task should access. However you create the policy, save it as scope-down-policy.json . If you want to continue calling GetScopedCredentials with the resulting credentials, also include the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in the Allow block of the permission policy. Step 2: Call GetScopedCredentials Pass the scope down policy you created to GetScopedCredentials. The following command also uses the optional duration-seconds parameter to limit the resulting session duration and the optional scoped-session-description parameter to record context for the scoped-down credentials. If you omit the duration-seconds parameter, the credentials keep the calling session’s remaining duration. aws sts get-scoped-credentials \ --policy '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"}]}' \ --duration-seconds 300 \ --scoped-session-description report-status-job \ --region us-west-2 The response includes a new set of temporary security credentials, a SessionInfo element, and some helpful information about session size and contents. { "Credentials": { "AccessKeyId": "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE", "SecretAccessKey": "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY, "SessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...", "Expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z" }, "SessionInfo": { "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane", "ScopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane" }, "SessionTokenUtilization": 17, "SessionTokenSize": 724, "ScopedPoliciesCount": 1 } Notice that the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the SessionInfo element matches the ARN of your calling session. The scoped-down credentials retain the identity of the calling session, including the role session name, session tags and context keys. The ScopedPoliciesCount value in the response shows how many scope down policies apply to the session. It increases only when a recursive call adds a new scope down policy and not when a call only shortens the session duration. Each GetScopedCredentials call is logged in AWS CloudTrail . The following event, shortened for readability, shows the call from this example. { "eventVersion": "1.11", "userIdentity": { "type": "AssumedRole", "principalId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:janee", "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane", "accessKeyId": "ASIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE", ... }, "eventTime": "2026-10-12T02:55:00Z", "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com", "eventName": "GetScopedCredentials", "awsRegion": "us-west-2", ... "requestParameters": { "policy": "{\"Version\":\"2012-10-17\",\"Statement\":[{\"Effect\":\"Allow\",\"Action\":\"s3:GetObject\",\"Resource\":\"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*\"}]}", "scopedSessionDescription": "report-status-job", "durationSeconds": 300 }, "responseElements": { "credentials": { "accessKeyId": "ASIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE", "sessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...", "expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z" }, "sessionInfo": { "scopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane", "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane" }, "sessionTokenUtilization": 17, "sessionTokenSize": 724, "scopedPoliciesCount": 1 }, "readOnly": false, ... } The scopedSessionDescription value in the CloudTrail event records the text you passed to the API call earlier. Later calls made with the scoped-down credentials show the scoped down session’s access key ID in userIdentity.accessKeyId , which can be used to trace back to its immediate parent session. Step 3 (optional): Scope down the credentials again You can call GetScopedCredentials recursively with the scoped-down credentials to narrow permissions or reduce session duration even further. You can apply a maximum of three scope down policies to a session, and each new scope down policy intersects with all prior ones. Recursive calls that only shorten the session duration and don’t add a scope down policy don’t count toward this limit. For a recursive call to succeed, every earlier scope down policy must allow the sts:GetScopedCredentials action. Managing access to GetScopedCredentials You can control access to the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in all relevant policy types. You can also use the sts:DurationSeconds condition key to limit the session duration of scoped-down credentials, and global condition keys such as aws:PrincipalArn , aws:PrincipalTag , and aws:SourceVpce to restrict who can call the API and from where. Availability and request quota GetScopedCredentials is available in all AWS commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. The API has a dedicated request quota of 200 requests per second per account in each Region at launch. You can use scoped-down credentials with most AWS services. For a list of services that aren’t supported, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference . Conclusion GetScopedCredentials gives you a building block for reducing permissions at runtime. This is particularly helpful when you want to give each agent, sub agent or workload only the access it needs. For more information about GetScopedCredentials, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference . To learn how permissions are evaluated for scoped-down credentials, see Permissions for GetScopedCredentials and Policy evaluation for requests within a single account . Now go build! If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below. If you have questions about this post, start a new thread on AWS re:Post or contact AWS Support . Vaishnavi Merugu Vaishnavi is a Senior Technical Product Manager in AWS Identity. Her work focuses on products that simplify identity and access management for customers. Outside of work, she enjoys traveling and exploring new cultures and food. Ryan Peng Ryan is a Software Development Engineer in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), where he builds the short-term credential vending systems that customers rely on to grant and constrain access to their AWS resources. Most recently, he has focused on how workloads and AI agents can run with the narrowest set of permissions they need. Outside of work, Ryan enjoys watching and playing sports, and staying active outdoors.

Similarly, the session duration you request can’t exceed the remaining duration of the calling session. You can also call GetScopedCredentials again with the resulting credentials to scope down permissions or reduce session duration even further.

GetScopedCredentials is designed as a building block. In this post, we walk through a few common use cases to get you started, show you how to call GetScopedCredentials, and explain how to manage access to it.

Example use cases

You can use GetScopedCredentials whenever a workload needs narrower access than the session that starts it. Examples include limiting what AI agents can do, scoping down permissions based on runtime context, and granting just-in-time access. We cover two of the most common use cases in more detail in this section.

Limit what AI agents can do

When you pass credentials to an agent, the agent can use any permission those credentials carry. An agent decides which actions to take at runtime, often based on prompts or tool output. If its credentials are overly permissive, an agent that makes a mistake can act beyond the task you gave it.

Before you pass credentials to an agent, you can use GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions to only what its tasks require, such as read access to a single Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket. You could also take the opposite approach and keep most of its permissions while removing only the actions the agent should never perform, such as deleting resources. An orchestrating agent can do the same for each sub-agent it starts. Because a scope down operation can only narrow permissions, a sub-agent never has more access than the agent that started it. To help ensure that your agents only have access to the scoped-down credentials, run them in isolated or sandbox environments such as AWS Strands Box.

Scope down permissions based on runtime context

Many workloads run under a single IAM role but need different, narrower permissions for each task they perform. The right set of permissions for a task often depends on information the workload learns only at runtime, such as who sent a request.

Consider a multi-tenant application that stores each tenant’s files under a separate prefix in one S3 bucket. This application uses a single IAM role to serve all its tenants, so the role can access every tenant’s prefix. However, each request should reach only the files of the tenant who sent it, and the application learns which tenant that is only after it authenticates the request. At that point, a trusted credential broker in the application takes the tenant details from the authenticated session and calls GetScopedCredentials with a scope down policy that allows access only to that tenant’s prefix. It passes only the scoped-down credentials to the worker that handles the request, so Amazon S3 denies that worker access to other tenants’ prefixes even though the original role covers them all.

How to call GetScopedCredentials

This section walks through the process of scoping down permissions for an existing session. Before you call GetScopedCredentials, make sure you have valid temporary security credentials and that they have the permissions to call the API. The following identity based policy grants that permission.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "sts:GetScopedCredentials",
    "Resource": "*"
  }]
}

To call GetScopedCredentials, use the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDK for your programming language.

Step 1: Define a scope down policy

Write a scope down policy that describes the maximum permissions the resulting credentials should have. At launch, GetScopedCredentials accepts one inline scope down policy of up to 2,048 characters. You can write a scope down policy in many ways, such as authoring a policy from scratch, reusing or modifying an existing policy, or asking an AI assistant to draft one. This section covers two such approaches.

Option A: Write the policy yourself

If you know which actions and resources your task needs, write the policy directly. The following sample policy allows the resulting credentials to only read objects from a single S3 bucket.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"
  }]
}

Make sure to include every action the task needs, including dependent actions. For example, if your task uses Amazon Athena to query data in Amazon S3, the policy must also allow s3:GetObject on that data, because Athena reads it with your credentials.

To keep most of the calling session’s permissions and remove only a few sensitive ones, use an Allow statement with NotAction. This statement doesn’t grant additional access, because a scope down policy can only reduce permissions. The resulting credentials keep the calling session’s permissions except the actions you list, which makes this a quick way to set guardrails without listing each action a task needs. The following sample policy blocks identity and account management, assuming other roles, and deleting some critical resources.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "NotAction": [
      "iam:*",
      "organizations:*",
      "account:*",
      "sts:AssumeRole*",
      "s3:DeleteBucket",
      "ec2:TerminateInstances",
      "rds:DeleteDBInstance",
      "dynamodb:DeleteTable"
    ],
    "Resource": "*"
  }]
}

Option B: Generate the policy with IAM Policy Autopilot

You can also use IAM Policy Autopilot to generate a scope down policy. IAM Policy Autopilot is an open source tool from AWS that analyzes the AWS SDK calls in your code and identifies the permissions it requires to run successfully. You can run it from the command line or as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in your AI coding assistant. To install it, see the Getting Started instructions for IAM Policy Autopilot.

We’ll use the following Python code to generate a scope down policy using IAM Policy Autopilot. It records a report’s status in an Amazon DynamoDB table.

import json
import logging
import os

import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

dynamodb = boto3.client("dynamodb")
table_name = os.environ["TABLE_NAME"]


def _response(status_code, message):
    return {"statusCode": status_code, "body": json.dumps({"message": message})}


def handler(event, context):
    try:
        request = json.loads(event.get("body") or "{}")
        report_id = request["reportId"]
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, TypeError):
        return _response(400, "Request body must be JSON with a reportId")

    if not isinstance(report_id, str) or not report_id:
        return _response(400, "reportId must be a non-empty string")

    try:
        dynamodb.put_item(
            TableName=table_name,
            Item={
                "reportId": {"S": report_id},
                "status": {"S": "READY"},
            },
            ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(reportId)",
        )
        return _response(200, "Report status saved")
    except ClientError as error:
        code = error.response["Error"]["Code"]
        if code == "ConditionalCheckFailedException":
            return _response(409, "Report status already exists")

        logger.error("PutItem failed: %s", code)
        return _response(500, "Unable to save the report status")

Save the code as report_status.py and run the following command. If the generated policy exceeds the 2,048 character limit, set the max-policy-size and allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size options to 2048. IAM Policy Autopilot then replaces groups of actions with wildcards to fit that size and warns you if it can’t.

iam-policy-autopilot generate-policies ./report_status.py \
  --region us-west-2 \
  --account 123456789012 \
  --service-hints dynamodb \
  --max-policy-size 2048 \
  --allow-overpermissive-wildcards-to-limit-total-output-size 2048 \
  --pretty

IAM Policy Autopilot returns the following policy.

{
  "Id": "IamPolicyAutopilot",
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "dynamodb:PutItem",
        "dynamodb:WriteDataForReplication"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-west-2:123456789012:table/*"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "kms:Decrypt"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789012:key/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:ViaService": [
            "dynamodb.us-west-2.amazonaws.com"
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

IAM Policy Autopilot generates a starting policy that can include wildcards, either because specific resources can’t be inferred from the code, such as with the table/* and key/* resources in this example, or because an optional parameter that limits policy size replaced actions with wildcards. Review the generated policies and replace the wildcards with the actions and resources your task should access.

However you create the policy, save it as scope-down-policy.json. If you want to continue calling GetScopedCredentials with the resulting credentials, also include the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in the Allow block of the permission policy.

Step 2: Call GetScopedCredentials

Pass the scope down policy you created to GetScopedCredentials. The following command also uses the optional duration-seconds parameter to limit the resulting session duration and the optional scoped-session-description parameter to record context for the scoped-down credentials. If you omit the duration-seconds parameter, the credentials keep the calling session’s remaining duration.

aws sts get-scoped-credentials \
  --policy '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*"}]}' \
  --duration-seconds 300 \
  --scoped-session-description report-status-job \
  --region us-west-2

The response includes a new set of temporary security credentials, a SessionInfo element, and some helpful information about session size and contents.

{
  "Credentials": {
    "AccessKeyId": "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE",
    "SecretAccessKey": "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY,
    "SessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...",
    "Expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z"
  },
  "SessionInfo": {
    "Arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane",
    "ScopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane"
  },
  "SessionTokenUtilization": 17,
  "SessionTokenSize": 724,
  "ScopedPoliciesCount": 1
}

Notice that the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the SessionInfo element matches the ARN of your calling session. The scoped-down credentials retain the identity of the calling session, including the role session name, session tags and context keys.

The ScopedPoliciesCount value in the response shows how many scope down policies apply to the session. It increases only when a recursive call adds a new scope down policy and not when a call only shortens the session duration.

Each GetScopedCredentials call is logged in AWS CloudTrail. The following event, shortened for readability, shows the call from this example.

{
    "eventVersion": "1.11",
    "userIdentity": {
        "type": "AssumedRole",
        "principalId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:janee",
        "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane",
        "accessKeyId": "ASIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE",
        ...
    },
    "eventTime": "2026-10-12T02:55:00Z",
    "eventSource": "sts.amazonaws.com",
    "eventName": "GetScopedCredentials",
    "awsRegion": "us-west-2",
    ...
    "requestParameters": {
        "policy": "{\"Version\":\"2012-10-17\",\"Statement\":[{\"Effect\":\"Allow\",\"Action\":\"s3:GetObject\",\"Resource\":\"arn:aws:s3:::amzn-s3-demo-bucket/*\"}]}",
        "scopedSessionDescription": "report-status-job",
        "durationSeconds": 300
    },
    "responseElements": {
        "credentials": {
            "accessKeyId": "ASIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE",
            "sessionToken": "IQoJb3JpZ2luX2VjEHMaCXVzL...",
            "expiration": "2026-10-12T03:00:00Z"
        },
        "sessionInfo": {
            "scopedSessionId": "AROADBQP57FF2AEXAMPLE:jane",
            "arn": "arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/Developer/jane"
        },
        "sessionTokenUtilization": 17,
        "sessionTokenSize": 724,
        "scopedPoliciesCount": 1
    },
    "readOnly": false,
    ...
}

The scopedSessionDescription value in the CloudTrail event records the text you passed to the API call earlier. Later calls made with the scoped-down credentials show the scoped down session’s access key ID in userIdentity.accessKeyId, which can be used to trace back to its immediate parent session.

Step 3 (optional): Scope down the credentials again

You can call GetScopedCredentials recursively with the scoped-down credentials to narrow permissions or reduce session duration even further. You can apply a maximum of three scope down policies to a session, and each new scope down policy intersects with all prior ones. Recursive calls that only shorten the session duration and don’t add a scope down policy don’t count toward this limit. For a recursive call to succeed, every earlier scope down policy must allow the sts:GetScopedCredentials action.

Managing access to GetScopedCredentials

You can control access to the sts:GetScopedCredentials action in all relevant policy types. You can also use the sts:DurationSeconds condition key to limit the session duration of scoped-down credentials, and global condition keys such as aws:PrincipalArn, aws:PrincipalTag, and aws:SourceVpce to restrict who can call the API and from where.

Availability and request quota

GetScopedCredentials is available in all AWS commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. The API has a dedicated request quota of 200 requests per second per account in each Region at launch. You can use scoped-down credentials with most AWS services. For a list of services that aren’t supported, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference.

Conclusion

GetScopedCredentials gives you a building block for reducing permissions at runtime. This is particularly helpful when you want to give each agent, sub agent or workload only the access it needs.

For more information about GetScopedCredentials, see the GetScopedCredentials API reference. To learn how permissions are evaluated for scoped-down credentials, see Permissions for GetScopedCredentials and Policy evaluation for requests within a single account. Now go build!

items.title: Beyond the phone: where confidence in evidence access drops
items.summary: Key takeaways More than eight in 10 digital evidence professionals who work with mobile data are very or extremely confident their organization can access it. For vehicle and drone data, fewer than half say the same. Mobile confidence had to be earned: when encryption upended acquisition, it took new tools and training to catch up. Vehicles and drones are now facing the same encryption challenges phones did. Closing the gap will take the same mix of tools and skills, and 58% say more training or technical expertise would improve access. Ask digital evidence professionals whether they can reach the data on a phone, and most will say yes. Ask about a vehicle or a drone, and the answer changes. In our Clearing the path to justice: 2027 public sector digital investigations report , 87% of the 306 public sector professionals we surveyed work with mobile device data, and more than eight in 10 of them are very or extremely confident their organization can access it. That confidence drops quickly when it comes to newer data sources. Among those who work with each source, the share who are very or extremely confident falls to: 46% for vehicle data 48% for drone data Confidence drops sharply for vehicle and drone data. Base: respondents who work with each evidence type. Mobile forensics went through a similar shift years ago, and vehicles and drones are now starting down that same road. How mobile forensics adapted to encryption About 15 years ago, physical methods like chip-off and JTAG were standard ways to acquire evidence from many phones: examiners opened the device and dumped the flash. Full-disk encryption largely ended that. Reading the data straight from the chip no longer returned what examiners needed, so they had to find ways into the phone while it was running to get the keys that decrypt the data. Encryption remains a persistent challenge, especially as operating systems keep evolving. Device encryption and passwords are still the most commonly cited obstacle to acquiring digital evidence (65%), and 51% point to devices that are locked, powered off , wiped, or otherwise inaccessible in the field. But purpose-built tools like Magnet Graykey have given examiners dependable ways in, and respondents’ confidence in mobile access reflects that. Device encryption and passwords are the most commonly cited barrier to acquiring digital evidence. Vehicle forensics: encryption reaches the infotainment system Until around 2020, most vehicles resembled those older phones. Data sat unencrypted, so an examiner could do a chip-off and read it in plain text. That’s changing as drivers expect navigation, apps, and smooth phone connections in their infotainment units. Those features need modern processors, and many units now use the same protections examiners know from mobile devices, such as secure boot and trusted execution environments. That puts vehicle chip-offs on the same path phone chip-offs took. A chip-off from one of these units may still return logs and system information, but high-value user data like contacts may be encrypted and unreadable. In mobile forensics, few examiners would rely on a chip-off today for that reason. Encryption varies by manufacturer and unit, and units with richer features are generally the ones encrypted at rest. That’s the catch for investigators: the vehicles most likely to hold useful evidence are also the ones legacy vehicle acquisition methods can’t reach. Removing the infotainment unit isn’t a reliable workaround either. Many units need to communicate with other parts of the vehicle when they start up, including to get the keys that unlock their data. What’s standing between digital evidence and justice? Drawing on insights from 300+ public sector professionals, the report explores why evidence is becoming harder to access, how disconnected handoffs delay cases, and what agencies need to strengthen trust in the age of AI. Read the report Drone forensics: encryption is spreading Drones aren’t only a military or federal concern. Local agencies have seen them used to deliver small quantities of narcotics and drop contraband into county jails. Yet drone forensics is still new territory for much of the digital forensics community. Part of the challenge is how fast the technology moves. Makes, models, and firmware change constantly, so the path into the data keeps shifting. Protections are changing too. For a long time, encryption was rare in drones, and even encrypted models weren’t encrypted at rest. Now more manufacturers are adding encryption, obfuscation, or modified compression. Manufacturers first worked out how to get a drone to fly, float, or drive. Now they’re working out how to secure it. Handling is where drones differ most from phones. With a phone, the goal is often to keep the device on and in its current state. With a drone, the priority is to render it safe and power it off. It may be carrying a dangerous payload, and some disassembly, such as removing the battery and propellers, may be needed for safety. Carrying mobile habits over to drones can cost a case. Internal storage is limited, so a drone left running can overwrite previous flight logs and sensor data, along with data that could have traced it back to where it came from. Closing the access gap for vehicles and drones Whatever the data source, access limitations can affect casework. Sixty-three percent of respondents say they have delayed investigations or case timelines, and 76% agree they can affect their ability to show evidence is complete if it’s challenged. When we asked what would most improve access, respondents pointed to both tools and skills: Faster support for new devices, operating systems, and apps (75%) Better handling of encrypted, locked, or powered-off devices (65%) More training or technical expertise (58%) Mobile forensics shows the gap can close when tools and training keep pace with encryption. Magnet Forensics is applying that lesson to newer data sources. Magnet Autokey helps examiners reach encrypted vehicle infotainment data over USB, without a teardown or chip-off, and V2 Forensics , which joined Magnet this year, brings dedicated drone forensics capabilities. Training matters beyond the lab, too. When investigators and first responders know how to handle a device at the scene, whether that means keeping a phone powered on or powering a drone off, they help preserve the data examiners need. Next steps Read the full report to see how access confidence varies across evidence sources, where evidence sharing breaks down between handoffs, and how AI-generated media is testing trust in evidence. Then join Brandon Epstein and Jeff Rutherford on Dec. 2 for a closer look at the barriers between evidence and answers.

items.title: How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
items.summary: On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell ( CVE-2026-132825 ), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 . The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure. Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases. The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing . Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise. What we know about ruby2shell Ruby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length. The German sharp s (ß) breaks that assumption. Its uppercase form is two characters, SS. In 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, Ruby writes those two bytes but checks for room for only one. According to Veria Labs, a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. The methods that reach the bug are upcase , swapcase , downcase(:fold) and casecmp? . UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected. A one-byte overflow can look harmless. In a memory-corruption exploit, though, a single byte written past the end of a heap buffer can be enough to corrupt an adjacent object or allocator metadata. Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after. Why default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposed HTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a _method parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of _method to uppercase. Rails includes this middleware by default, and classic-style Sinatra applications enable it. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose _method part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs. Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from. Who is affected Condition Details Ruby version Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix. Framework Rails and classic-style Sinatra in their default configuration. Any other code that changes the case of attacker-controlled strings in a legacy single-byte encoding. Bundled software As of November 19, 2026, Veria Labs lists GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 as bundling an affected Ruby in their latest release. Discourse moved its Docker base image to Ruby 4.0.10 on November 19, so rebuilding a Docker install picks up the fix. Distribution packages can backport fixes without changing the Ruby version number, so check the full package version against your distribution's advisory. Six more Ruby flaws in the same release Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 also fix six other memory safety flaws , and Ruby says several of them can lead to code execution. One, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, is an integer overflow in the same string case conversion code, and our second WAF rule covers it. The other five are in Ruby's regular expression engine. Most of them require the application to compile or match a regular expression pattern supplied by the attacker. That is uncommon in web applications, but it does happen in search features, filtering rules and admin tools. How Cloudflare WAF protects you Upgrading every Ruby runtime takes time, especially when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products and container images. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch. New managed rules, on for every customer Both rules are part of the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee), with Block as the default action. Rule description Rule ID Ruleset Default action Ruby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-132825 7328f23691e44b07892ebd25b19210f1 Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan) Block Ruby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-132825 1afa543a1ed84893b01df04c34402c88 Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans) Block Ruby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px 8660e37e86444f9f9267ba22e9855f05 Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan) Block Ruby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px 6defac6a52334542adf4a162daf25922 Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans) Block On the Free plan, the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset runs automatically, so there is nothing to turn on. On paid plans, the rules are active wherever the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed. Because paid plans give you more control over how rulesets are deployed, the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset may not be active on every zone. We recommend checking its status to confirm that it is running. You can use the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules in your dashboard. What the WAF cannot see A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious input arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable code: Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. Requests sent directly to your origin IP address, and traffic between internal services, never reach the WAF. Configure your origin to accept traffic only from Cloudflare, for example with Cloudflare Tunnel or Authenticated Origin Pulls . Other entry points into the same code. Ruby code that changes the case of strings from email, file imports, message queues or background jobs can reach ruby2shell without an HTTP request. Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score Memory corruption is usually only the first step. To run commands, an attacker still has to deliver a second-stage payload, such as shell commands or a reverse shell, and then interact with the compromised server. WAF attack score uses machine learning to score each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch exploit variations and post-exploitation traffic that signature-based rules can miss. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans. Impact on Cloudflare infrastructure Cloudflare has patched its systems that use Ruby against ruby2shell. We have found no indication of compromise and continue to monitor. Patch now ruby2shell turns a one-byte miscalculation in string case conversion into a pre-authentication path to code execution in default Rails and Sinatra apps. With a public proof of concept expected within days, the window to patch is short. Here is what to do: Check your WAF coverage. On the Free plan, the ruby2shell rules are already blocking. On paid plans, confirm the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and the rules have not been overridden. Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 and restart every Ruby process, including background workers. Rebuild container images. Move applications on Ruby 3.2 or earlier to a supported series. Update self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject and Chatwoot, as each vendor releases a fix. Rebuild Discourse Docker installs now. Inventory your runtimes. The Zero Wire briefing includes a prompt you can give an AI agent to find every affected Ruby runtime in your infrastructure. Our WAF analysts will keep updating protections as new techniques appear. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates.

You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise.

What we know about ruby2shell

Ruby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length.

Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after.

HTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a _method parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of _method to uppercase. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose _method part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs.

Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from.

Who is affected

Condition

Details

Ruby version

Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.

Most of them require the application to compile or match a regular expression pattern supplied by the attacker. That is uncommon in web applications, but it does happen in search features, filtering rules and admin tools.

How Cloudflare WAF protects you

Upgrading every Ruby runtime takes time, especially when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products and container images. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.

A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious input arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable code:

Memory corruption is usually only the first step. To run commands, an attacker still has to deliver a second-stage payload, such as shell commands or a reverse shell, and then interact with the compromised server. Patch now

ruby2shell turns a one-byte miscalculation in string case conversion into a pre-authentication path to code execution in default Rails and Sinatra apps. With a public proof of concept expected within days, the window to patch is short. Here is what to do:

  1. Check your WAF coverage. On the Free plan, the ruby2shell rules are already blocking. On paid plans, confirm the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and the rules have not been overridden.
  2. Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 and restart every Ruby process, including background workers. Rebuild container images. Move applications on Ruby 3.2 or earlier to a supported series.
  3. Update self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject and Chatwoot, as each vendor releases a fix. Rebuild Discourse Docker installs now.
  4. Inventory your runtimes. The Zero Wire briefing includes a prompt you can give an AI agent to find every affected Ruby runtime in your infrastructure.

Our WAF analysts will keep updating protections as new techniques appear. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates.

items.summary: On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714) , a vulnerability in PHP's default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project fixed it the same day in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases fix 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of them also rated critical. Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF) blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns, including for customers on the Free plan. The protection comes from a PHP remote code execution rule we first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities. That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell. The rule is part of both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, is enabled by default, and its default action is Block. In the same WAF release, we added three new rules to the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset for paid plans: one for a request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), and two for flaws in PHP's SOAP extension (CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506) that PHP fixed in the same releases. These rules are enabled by default with the Log action, because the request patterns they look for can also appear in legitimate traffic, and blocking by default could disrupt it. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the action to Block once they confirm the rules do not affect legitimate traffic. The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart every worker. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and follow how the vulnerabilities develop in the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing . There appears to be no indication so far that these vulnerabilities have been exploited. As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog , and no source we reviewed reports exploitation in the wild. What we know about phpAfterShell PHP stores session data in files by default. When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array. When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file. phpAfterShell is triggered when that write is interrupted. The session file can then hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the end of the old one. On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker controlled the old data, PHP can end up deserializing objects of the attacker's choice. An attacker trying to exploit the flaw is likely to first search for a way to place controlled data in the session. PHP's advisory names two: Session upload progress , a PHP feature that writes information about a running file upload into the session. A remote client can use it to shape the stored data. Applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session . According to PHP, code execution also requires an interruption at a useful point in the write and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application. depthfirst reports that it reached code execution without an application gadget by chaining a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. The sources we reviewed do not establish whether that second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases. depthfirst says it discovered and reported phpAfterShell. The CVE record credits Leo Lin and Asahi as reporters. The other critical flaws The same releases fix six more critical vulnerabilities. Each one needs a specific configuration to be exploitable: CVE Component Impact Conditions CVE-2026-129289 PHP-FPM An unauthenticated attacker can smuggle a second FastCGI request into PHP-FPM and run PHP code as the worker. A front end that reuses backend FastCGI connections (nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, or HAProxy), an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end, and the path of an existing PHP script. CVE-2026-115560 Session serializer Object injection through a mismatch between session serializers. First covered in our php2shell briefing, now fixed. Session upload progress enabled. PHP widened the scope: applications, pools or command-line jobs that use different serializers and share a session store are affected. CVE-2026-129496 Timezone cache Use-after-free that can crash a fresh worker and possibly run code. PHP demonstrated code execution locally with known memory addresses. Non-thread-safe builds where a startup diagnostic has been written to a PHP error log file. CVE-2026-129481 Session shutdown Use-after-free, described by PHP as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619. No code execution demonstrated. PHP 8.3 and later. CVE-2026-129474 Fatal error backtraces Use-after-free in magic method backtraces. PHP 8.5 and later, where fatal error backtraces are enabled by default. Setting zend.exception_ignore_args=1, the php.ini-production default, blocks the demonstrated attack. CVE-2026-129182 Fatal error backtraces Use-after-free. No code execution demonstrated. PHP 8.5, specific path-level settings, and an Apache per-directory configuration or front end that produces an early diagnostic. Who is affected The vulnerable versions are PHP 8.2 before 8.2.36, 8.3 before 8.3.37, 8.4 before 8.4.28, 8.5 before 8.5.13, and the 8.6.0 release candidates. Whether a deployment is exposed depends on the conditions of each flaw. PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life. depthfirst says the official 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 end-of-life mitigation branches are not affected by phpAfterShell, but PHP says CVE-2026-129289 was introduced in PHP 5.6.0 and that releases older than 8.2 may also be affected by CVE-2026-115560. Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the PHP version number. Check the full package version against your distribution's advisory. How Cloudflare WAF protects you PHP runs a large share of the web, often inside content management systems, plugins, and container images that teams do not update directly. Patching every PHP runtime takes time. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch. phpAfterShell: protection on every plan We released the original PHP remote code execution rules in an emergency release on October 21, 2026, after the php2shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) were disclosed. Because of that overlap, the existing rule already matched part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before disclosure. On November 19, we updated the rule's detection logic to cover phpAfterShell and added CVE-2026-126714 to its description. Rule description Rule ID Ruleset Default action PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714) #6 19373a83abb840e18ab3ce5a7975ce1b Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan) Block PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714) #6 4148ae686fdb4d01be673fab9d9c073d Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans) Block Free plan customers do not need to take any action. On paid plans, the rule is active wherever the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed. You can use the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules in your dashboard. New rules for PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws The three new rules are part of the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee) and are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans. Rule description Rule ID Default action PHP-FPM - CVE:CVE-2026-129289 8ef1c34a424b4ccfa6f6fe186c6f42b2 Log PHP SOAP - CVE:CVE-2026-15353 5c5a9d6397e44837a3214b5ba54028d4 Log PHP SOAP - CVE:CVE-2026-129506 00a23de67a684876ba67c5d44521b819 Log To review their matches, go to Security > Analytics > Events and filter by rule ID. If the matches are not legitimate traffic, change the rule action to Block: go to Security > Settings, edit the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, search for the CVE identifier and set the rule action to Block, or you can refer to the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules configuration. What the WAF cannot see A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious data arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to these vulnerabilities, including: The deserialization step. phpAfterShell's final step happens inside PHP, when it reads a corrupted session file. The WAF can block the requests that plant the payload, not the read itself. Session data from other sources. If an application copies user-controlled data into the session from a database, a queue or an upstream API, that data may never cross the WAF in a recognizable form. Flaws triggered by server state. CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 depend on error logs, diagnostics and worker lifecycle. They do not have dedicated WAF rules, and the patch and the configuration changes below are the way to address them. Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services and PHP-FPM listeners exposed directly to a network. Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score WAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for attack payloads. It is available on Business plans (cf.waf.score.class) and, with a dedicated remote code execution sub-score (cf.waf.score.rce) along with an overall score (cf.waf.score), on Enterprise plans. Attack score complements the managed rules. It will not recognize every serialized object or smuggled FastCGI record on its own, but a working exploit chain usually needs more than one request, and the later stages carry payloads the model is trained to score: Second-stage payloads. Once an attacker can run code, they still need to send commands: shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, system(), passthru()), PHP code evaluation (eval(), assert()) or reverse-shell strings in headers, query parameters or request bodies. Webshell traffic. Attackers often drop a small PHP webshell after the initial compromise. Requests that pass operating system commands to that webshell remain visible to attack score. Deploy protections and patch You can find more information on how to deploy managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide . In short: Check that phpAfterShell protection is active. On the Free plan, no action is needed. On paid plans, make sure the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and that the PHP Remote Code Execution Attack #6 rule is set to Block. Review the new rules and switch them to Block. The CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506 rules are in Log mode by default. Review their matches in Security Events, then change their action to Block. Layer attack score . Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with a low remote code execution score, for example cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans. CVE

A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious data arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to these vulnerabilities, including:

  • The deserialization step. phpAfterShell's final step happens inside PHP, when it reads a corrupted session file. The WAF can block the requests that plant the payload, not the read itself.
  • Session data from other sources. If an application copies user-controlled data into the session from a database, a queue or an upstream API, that data may never cross the WAF in a recognizable form.

  • Second-stage payloads. Once an attacker can run code, they still need to send commands: shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, system(), passthru()), PHP code evaluation (eval(), assert()) or reverse-shell strings in headers, query parameters or request bodies.

  4. Upgrade PHP. Move to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0. items.title: Chinese-nexus actor’s Cairn AI agents found a zero-day on their own
items.summary: Amazon Threat Intelligence is sharing findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor using autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The actor gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server. These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable. Discovery On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time. Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026. Cairn and an overview of this campaign Cairn was built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple. Given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. That same ease of use makes it attractive to threat actors. In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to “obtain shell access.” Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step. The campaign included several operations that varied widely in complexity and outcome. The following operations show both the persistence and the capability of autonomous AI agents. Persistence against a hardened target The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. Redis is a database that keeps frequently used data in memory so applications can retrieve it quickly, which can make it a valuable foothold inside a network. Over roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, the agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. These included abusing Redis’s replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted Log4Shell injection against another service running on the same system. When those attempts failed, the agents mapped the internal Docker network topology through a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance and launched credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and several other services. None of these attempts succeeded. A separate operation ran for more than 6 hours and targeted a university GPU server, which is a group of high-performance computers built for computing-intensive research. The agents first built a list of about 80 real usernames by researching the university’s public presence, including faculty directories, lab websites, archived web pages, and academic papers. Then, they tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against the server’s remote login (SSH), and, on other systems across the university network, an admin dashboard, a network storage device, a VPN server, and the university’s campus portal. They never found a working login. Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction. Zero-day discovery Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server. items.summary_html:
Amazon Threat Intelligence is sharing findings from an investigation into a Chinese-nexus threat actor using autonomous AI agents to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement. The actor gave the agents a simple goal: “obtain shell access.” During the campaign, the agents found a zero-day in an open-source application and used it to gain full control of a server. These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable.

Discovery

On September 10, 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn, an open-source autonomous AI penetration-testing framework, running without authentication. Because the operator left the server publicly accessible, the operational history of the platform was visible to anyone on the internet, including project configurations, actor prompts, and AI output. The operator wrote prompts in Simplified Chinese, and the timestamps in executed scripts were configured to China Standard Time.

Analysis of the instance revealed a campaign targeting IP addresses associated with universities in East Asia outside mainland China over an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026.

Cairn and an overview of this campaign

Cairn was built as a research and problem-solving engine for defenders. Operating it is simple. Given a starting point and an objective in plain language, it coordinates multiple AI agents to find a path to that goal. That same ease of use makes it attractive to threat actors. In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to “obtain shell access.” Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step.

The campaign included several operations that varied widely in complexity and outcome. The following operations show both the persistence and the capability of autonomous AI agents.

Persistence against a hardened target

The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. Redis is a database that keeps frequently used data in memory so applications can retrieve it quickly, which can make it a valuable foothold inside a network. Over roughly 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, the agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. These included abusing Redis’s replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted Log4Shell injection against another service running on the same system.

When those attempts failed, the agents mapped the internal Docker network topology through a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance and launched credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and several other services. None of these attempts succeeded.

A separate operation ran for more than 6 hours and targeted a university GPU server, which is a group of high-performance computers built for computing-intensive research. The agents first built a list of about 80 real usernames by researching the university’s public presence, including faculty directories, lab websites, archived web pages, and academic papers. Then, they tested more than 30,000 credential combinations against the server’s remote login (SSH), and, on other systems across the university network, an admin dashboard, a network storage device, a VPN server, and the university’s campus portal. They never found a working login.

Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction.

Zero-day discovery

Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.

In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup. The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root.

At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.

Subsequent use

In another session, the threat actor stepped in. After the agents discovered the zero-day, the actor then provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network. The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel. The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.

Attribution

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that this is a Chinese-nexus threat actor based on the Simplified Chinese prompts, the China Standard Time script timestamps, and the targeting of universities likely of strategic interest to China.

Actions taken by AWS

Amazon Threat Intelligence notified the project’s maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a GitHub Security Advisory.

The affected organizations were non-AWS customers that AWS had no direct path to notify. Instead, AWS worked with a government partner to notify the organizations about the activity.

Adoption is growing

Gambit Security was one of the first organizations in the industry to document the use of Cairn by a threat group. Its research describes a separate, financially motivated actor using Cairn to target online retailers. Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations. Additional details are available in Gambit Security’s report.

What this means for defenders

The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response. An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints. To keep pace, organizations should prioritize high-confidence detections that trigger automated response, with humans overseeing outcomes rather than reviewing every individual action.

Behind the scenes, AWS active defense systems use global honeypots (decoy systems that attract threat actors) and network traffic analysis to identify actors that are scanning for vulnerable systems, and then help restrict that activity at the network level. These protections are built into the AWS network at no extra cost to customers.

Indicators of compromise

The following addresses appear in records dated September 8 to 10, 2026.

142[.]4.98.145

142[.]4.107.34
