items.summary: Executive Summary Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap out-of-bounds write in HotSpot’s AVX-512 Base64 decoder on x86-64. Calif reported it and showed pre-auth RCE in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Nobody has reported exploitation in the wild as of November 17, 2026. CISA issued an alert that same day, urging everyone to patch now. Your Java4Shell Response Plan Patch to Oracle 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, or 27.0.1.1, or to your vendor’s build with JDK-8393212. If you can’t patch today, start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restart it. You’re only exposed on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. ARM64 isn’t affected. Tip for Qualys customers: you can apply the step 2 flag with TruRisk Eliminate, targeting only the hosts that need it and rolling it back in one click. Affected Java Builds and Their Fixed Releases Oracle shipped the fixed builds on November 17, 2026. October’s builds are still vulnerable. Product Range Vulnerable Fixed build (Oracle) Oracle Java SE / OpenJDK 17 17.0.6 to 17.0.21 17.0.21.1 Oracle Java SE / OpenJDK 21 Below 21.0.13.1 21.0.13.1 Oracle Java SE / OpenJDK 25 Below 25.0.5.1 25.0.5.1 Oracle Java SE / OpenJDK 27 Below 27.0.1.1 27.0.1.1 OpenJDK (end of life) 18 to 20, 22 to 24, 26 All None. Move to a supported line Oracle Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack 8 8u511-perf 8u513-perf Oracle GraalVM for JDK 17 / 21 Below the fix 17.0.21.1 / 21.0.13.1 Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3 Below the fix 21.3.20.1 Distro packages built before the fix are vulnerable even when the version looks current. Ubuntu’s 17.0.21.0.3 and Oracle Linux’s 17.0.21 are two examples. How the Java4Shell Attack Chain Works This is a typical Java4Shell attack chain: The attacker needs a Base64 decode value they can control. Vulnerability discoverers were able to reach this pre-authentication condition via authentication in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after login in Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. A Java client that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server is exposed too. The attacker then sends valid decodes until the server compiler compiles the fast path, then the bad input: 64 valid characters and one =, or 128 and one = on older 17 builds. The target must pass the gates in the source. The JVM must see avx512_vbmi and avx512bw with UseAVX=3, the intrinsic must be on, and on 17u the input must be longer than 128 characters. The stub’s tail handling goes wrong. The next section walks through it. On a fixed build, or with the intrinsic off, nothing happens. Otherwise, 62 or 63 bytes land past the destination array on the Java heap. Vulnerability researchers mentioned that they groomed the heap (G1 regions, thread-local allocation buffers) to turn that write into code execution. Unsuccessful exploitation will lead to a denial-of-service condition on the endpoint. This remote code execution chain has only been mentioned as achieved by the vulnerability researchers. Nobody has reported it in the wild yet. Tracing Java4Shell to Its Root Cause Based on the jdk17u source at the fix commit, HotSpot generates the stub in generate_base64_decodeBlock (it shows up as implDecode at runtime), and C2 calls it from java.util.Base64$Decoder.decode0 once that method is hot. JDK-8268276 added the AVX-512 decoder in JDK 18 and JDK-8296735 backported it to 17.0.6, so 17.0.5 and older are clean. The whole vector decoder sits inside if (VM_Version::supports_avx512_vbmi() && VM_Version::supports_avx512bw()). Without both features HotSpot only builds the scalar 4-character loop, which is fine. 17u has no AVX2 decoder; the AVX2 tables in that file are for encoding. MIME input goes straight to the scalar loop. Basic and URL input take the vector path once it’s longer than 128 characters. The vector code decodes 64 characters a pass, and L_finalBit handles the last 1 to 63. Before the fix, a tail of 1 to 3 characters ending in = gave an output size of 0, and the padding step subtracted 1 from it. The output mask then came from bzhiq with an index of -1. bzhiq only reads the low 8 bits of the index, so -1 became 255, nothing got cleared and the mask stayed all ones. The final masked store wrote a full 64 bytes where it should have written none. The exact trigger condition on 17u follows from the control flow. The input must be longer than 128 characters and go through the basic or URL decoder, since MIME goes to the scalar loop. Inputs of 256 characters or more run through 256-character passes, then everything runs through 64-character passes, so the tail left at L_finalBit is the length modulo 64. Every character in those passes must be valid Base64; a = or any other bad character inside a pass makes the stub exit early and hand the rest to Java. The tail must be 1 to 3 characters ending in =, and any non-padding character in it must also be valid. Put together, the bad lengths are 64k + 1 to 64k + 3 for k of 2 or more: 129 to 131, 193 to 195, 257 to 259 and so on. Legitimate padded Base64 always has a length that’s a multiple of 4, so none of these inputs is valid anyway. Unpadded values such as JWT segments can have other lengths, but they never end in =. That makes length modulo 64 plus a trailing = a tighter hunting signal than “not a multiple of 4”. The fix, JDK-8393212, adds four lines at L_finalBit: if fewer than 4 characters remain, jump to L_bruteForce, the scalar path. The commit title is “Base64 optimization improvements”, which tells you nothing. The fix closes the underflow and causes no other change. The new check runs before the stub computes either the input mask or the output size. With 4 or more characters left, the output size starts at (length / 4) × 3, which is at least 3. Padding takes off at most 2, so the size stays at 1 or more and bzhiq always gets a valid index. A tail made only of = fails the validity check and drops to the scalar loop. Tails of 1 to 3 characters never reach the vector code at all. I checked memory safety only. I didn’t check whether the stub decodes every odd-length tail of 4 to 63 characters correctly, and the fix doesn’t touch that logic. No CWE is assigned yet. I’d file it as an integer underflow (CWE-191) that causes an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Windows x64 gets the same vector code; the function only differs in how it reads its arguments there. I’ve only read the 17u source. Calif’s shorter trigger on newer lines suggests a lower threshold than 128 characters there, but I haven’t confirmed it. Confirm Exposure From Inside the Java Runtime A JVM is exposed only when all four of these conditions are true: It runs on an x86-64 CPU with avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2. That covers Intel Ice Lake, Sapphire, Emerald and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 and newer. Skylake-SP and Cascade Lake have AVX-512 but no VBMI. It’s OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or 18 to 27, below the fixed builds. Oracle’s 8u511 Enterprise Performance Pack counts too, because it ships a 17-based VM. UseAVX=3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics=true, which are the defaults on those CPUs. Attacker input reaches the basic or URL decoder in java.util.Base64. Basic auth and JWT parsing do this before login. A quiet service isn’t safe. The attacker warms up C2 with valid decodes first. The OS doesn’t change the bug. Windows x64 gets the same generated code as Linux, though only Linux has public testing. I wouldn’t rely on /proc/cpuinfo. It doesn’t exist outside Linux, and an empty result looks like “not affected”. Ask the JVM what it sees instead, on any OS: java -Xlog:os+cpu -version 2>&1 | grep -oE ‘avx512f|avx512bw|avx512_vbmi|bmi2’ | sort -u java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep -E ‘ (UseAVX|UseBASE64Intrinsics) ‘ All four flags, UseAVX = 3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics = true mean that runtime is exposed. Run the check with each java binary on the host, since each runtime reports its own settings. Turn the intrinsic off with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restart the JVM. With that flag HotSpot never generates the stub, which I confirmed in the source and on a live JVM. Oracle hasn’t published it as a workaround. Control Impact Trade-off -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics Low Base64 decoding falls back to plain Java and runs slower. No one has published a number -XX:UseAVX=2 High Also stops it, since the VBMI decoder never gets built, but it drops every AVX-512 optimization. ARM64 JVMs won’t start with it Move to non-VBMI or ARM hosts High Migration work, and a reschedule back onto a VBMI node re-exposes you Skip -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock. Upwind reports it fails unless you also pass -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions. CISA’s alert also suggests validating Base64 at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. Boundary validation helps if it rejects padded input whose length isn’t a multiple of 4 before the decoder runs. Size limits won’t: the trigger is 65 characters on newer lines, shorter than most Basic-auth and JWT values. Limiting unauthenticated access works, but it means network ACLs or a VPN in front, because the vulnerable decode happens before login. Mitigate Java4Shell with TruRisk Eliminate For Qualys customers, the Java4Shell mitigation is available now with TruRisk Eliminate on Linux and Windows hosts, linked to QIDs such as 389494. As additional QIDs are released for different operating systems, we will test them and add support. The Cloud Agent runs it on the hosts you pick. Before it changes anything, it checks that the host has an AVX-512 VBMI CPU and an affected Java runtime, so hosts that can’t hit the bug are left alone. On the hosts that can, it adds -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and keeps whatever value was already there. The setting takes effect when each JVM restarts, so plan restarts with the application owners. Windows services pick it up after a host reboot. After the change, the agent reports every running Java process with its effective setting, worked out in the order HotSpot applies options. A JVM it can’t read shows up as unknown, so you know where to look instead of assuming it’s covered. Rollback is one click in the console and restores the previous value. The mitigation doesn’t reach containers; set the flag in the image or pod spec for those. Treat it as a bridge to the patched builds, since Oracle hasn’t published the flag as a workaround. Code execution is not the only outcome. A successful exploit chain can read Java heap memory before it runs any attacker code. That memory can hold private keys, tokens, and personal data. CISA also warns that crafted input can crash the JVM, so availability is at risk too. Java clients are exposed as well. The researchers report a client-side exploit in which a Java program is compromised simply by connecting over TLS to a malicious server. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)? Java4Shell is a heap out-of-bounds write in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder of the HotSpot JVM on x86-64. A malformed Base64 value can make the decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of an array on the Java heap. Researchers turned that into pre-authentication remote code execution in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. Which Java versions are affected by Java4Shell? OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, and versions 18 to 27, are affected below the fixed builds. Oracle’s 8u511 Enterprise Performance Pack is also affected because it uses a 17-based VM. Oracle released the fixed builds on November 17, 2026: 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1 and 8u513-perf. Vendor builds that include fix JDK-8393212 are also safe. Java 8 standard and Java 11 are not affected. Is Java4Shell being exploited in the wild? No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of November 17, 2026. Remote code execution has only been demonstrated by researchers. CISA issued an alert the same day urging organizations to patch now. How do I know if my Java runtime is exposed to Java4Shell? A Java runtime is exposed only when all four conditions are true. It runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. It’s an affected version. UseAVX=3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics are on, which are the defaults on those CPUs. And attacker input reaches the Basic or URL Base64 decoder. Check by asking each Java binary what it sees, not by reading /proc/cpuinfo . ARM64 is not affected. How can I close the Java4Shell vulnerability if I can’t patch yet? You can mitigate it by starting the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restarting it. With this flag, HotSpot never generates the vulnerable code. Oracle hasn’t published it as an official workaround, so treat it as a bridge until you can patch. How do I mitigate Java4Shell with TruRisk Eliminate? Apply -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics with TruRisk Eliminate through the Qualys Cloud Agent. It automatically targets only Linux and Windows hosts that have an AVX-512 VBMI CPU and an affected Java runtime. It keeps existing JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS values, reports the effective setting for every running Java process and offers one-click rollback.

I didn’t check whether the stub decodes every odd-length tail of 4 to 63 characters correctly, and the fix doesn’t touch that logic. 

No CWE is assigned yet. I’d file it as an integer underflow (CWE-191) that causes an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Windows x64 gets the same vector code; the function only differs in how it reads its arguments there. I’ve only read the 17u source. Calif’s shorter trigger on newer lines suggests a lower threshold than 128 characters there, but I haven’t confirmed it. 

Confirm Exposure From Inside the Java Runtime 

A JVM is exposed only when all four of these conditions are true: 

  1. It runs on an x86-64 CPU with avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2. That covers Intel Ice Lake, Sapphire, Emerald and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 and newer. Skylake-SP and Cascade Lake have AVX-512 but no VBMI. 
  2. It’s OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later, or 18 to 27, below the fixed builds. Oracle’s 8u511 Enterprise Performance Pack counts too, because it ships a 17-based VM. 
  3. UseAVX=3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics=true, which are the defaults on those CPUs. 
  4. Attacker input reaches the basic or URL decoder in java.util.Base64. Basic auth and JWT parsing do this before login. 

A quiet service isn’t safe. The attacker warms up C2 with valid decodes first. 

The OS doesn’t change the bug. Windows x64 gets the same generated code as Linux, though only Linux has public testing. 

I wouldn’t rely on /proc/cpuinfo. It doesn’t exist outside Linux, and an empty result looks like “not affected”. Ask the JVM what it sees instead, on any OS: 
java -Xlog:os+cpu -version 2>&1 | grep -oE ‘avx512f|avx512bw|avx512_vbmi|bmi2’ | sort -u 
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep -E ‘ (UseAVX|UseBASE64Intrinsics) ‘ 

All four flags, UseAVX = 3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics = true mean that runtime is exposed. Run the check with each java binary on the host, since each runtime reports its own settings. 

Turn the intrinsic off with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restart the JVM. With that flag HotSpot never generates the stub, which I confirmed in the source and on a live JVM. Oracle hasn’t published it as a workaround. 

Control Impact Trade-off -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics Low Base64 decoding falls back to plain Java and runs slower. No one has published a number -XX:UseAVX=2 High Also stops it, since the VBMI decoder never gets built, but it drops every AVX-512 optimization. ARM64 JVMs won’t start with it Move to non-VBMI or ARM hosts High Migration work, and a reschedule back onto a VBMI node re-exposes you 

Skip -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock. Upwind reports it fails unless you also pass -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions. 

CISA’s alert also suggests validating Base64 at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. Boundary validation helps if it rejects padded input whose length isn’t a multiple of 4 before the decoder runs. Size limits won’t: the trigger is 65 characters on newer lines, shorter than most Basic-auth and JWT values. Limiting unauthenticated access works, but it means network ACLs or a VPN in front, because the vulnerable decode happens before login.  

Mitigate Java4Shell with TruRisk Eliminate 

For Qualys customers, the Java4Shell mitigation is available now with TruRisk Eliminate on Linux and Windows hosts, linked to QIDs such as 389494. As additional QIDs are released for different operating systems, we will test them and add support. The Cloud Agent runs it on the hosts you pick. Before it changes anything, it checks that the host has an AVX-512 VBMI CPU and an affected Java runtime, so hosts that can’t hit the bug are left alone. On the hosts that can, it adds -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and keeps whatever value was already there. 

The setting takes effect when each JVM restarts, so plan restarts with the application owners. Windows services pick it up after a host reboot. After the change, the agent reports every running Java process with its effective setting, worked out in the order HotSpot applies options. A JVM it can’t read shows up as unknown, so you know where to look instead of assuming it’s covered. 

Rollback is one click in the console and restores the previous value. The mitigation doesn’t reach containers; set the flag in the image or pod spec for those. Treat it as a bridge to the patched builds, since Oracle hasn’t published the flag as a workaround. 

Code execution is not the only outcome. A successful exploit chain can read Java heap memory before it runs any attacker code. That memory can hold private keys, tokens, and personal data. CISA also warns that crafted input can crash the JVM, so availability is at risk too. Java clients are exposed as well. The researchers report a client-side exploit in which a Java program is compromised simply by connecting over TLS to a malicious server.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?
Java4Shell is a heap out-of-bounds write in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder of the HotSpot JVM on x86-64. A malformed Base64 value can make the decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of an array on the Java heap. Researchers turned that into pre-authentication remote code execution in Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.

Which Java versions are affected by Java4Shell?
OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, and versions 18 to 27, are affected below the fixed builds. Oracle’s 8u511 Enterprise Performance Pack is also affected because it uses a 17-based VM. Oracle released the fixed builds on November 17, 2026: 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1 and 8u513-perf. Vendor builds that include fix JDK-8393212 are also safe. Java 8 standard and Java 11 are not affected.

Is Java4Shell being exploited in the wild?
No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of November 17, 2026. Remote code execution has only been demonstrated by researchers. CISA issued an alert the same day urging organizations to patch now.

How do I know if my Java runtime is exposed to Java4Shell?
A Java runtime is exposed only when all four conditions are true. It runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. It’s an affected version. UseAVX=3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics are on, which are the defaults on those CPUs. And attacker input reaches the Basic or URL Base64 decoder. Check by asking each Java binary what it sees, not by reading /proc/cpuinfo. ARM64 is not affected.

How can I close the Java4Shell vulnerability if I can’t patch yet?
You can mitigate it by starting the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics and restarting it. With this flag, HotSpot never generates the vulnerable code. Oracle hasn’t published it as an official workaround, so treat it as a bridge until you can patch.

How do I mitigate Java4Shell with TruRisk Eliminate?
Apply -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics with TruRisk Eliminate through the Qualys Cloud Agent. It automatically targets only Linux and Windows hosts that have an AVX-512 VBMI CPU and an affected Java runtime. It keeps existing JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS values, reports the effective setting for every running Java process and offers one-click rollback.

items.title: Microsoft Investigates Attachment Upload Failures in New Outlook
items.summary: Microsoft is investigating reports that some Microsoft 365 users cannot upload email attachments in New Outlook. In a November 20 service update, the company said attachment uploads still work in Outlook on the web and classic Outlook. Microsoft is tracking the issue in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1561765. We're investigating reports of issues uploading attachments in New Outlook. Uploading attachments in Outlook on the web and Outlook classic are unaffected. For more information, see EX1561765 in the Microsoft 365 admin center. — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 20, 2026 New Outlook Attachment Issue The public update focused on uploads, but an Exchange Online advisory tracked by 365Fanatic says some users may also be unable to open attachments in New Outlook. Microsoft reproduced the issue internally and began reviewing diagnostic data to find the cause. The available updates did not identify affected regions, say how many users were impacted, or provide a timeline for a fix. The reported impact is narrower than the November 12–13 Microsoft 365 outage , which blocked mailbox access across several Outlook clients. In this case, Microsoft identified two alternatives for uploading files. The company has not publicly linked the attachment issue to the earlier outage. If a file will not upload in New Outlook, open the same mailbox in Outlook on the web or switch to classic Outlook if it is installed. Attach the file there and check that it appears in the message before sending. IT teams can follow Microsoft’s service health guide , then open Health → Service health in the admin center and look for EX1561765. Help desks can use the incident ID to group matching reports while noting cases that also fail in the browser or classic Outlook. Staff should verify any emailed recovery instructions with their help desk rather than follow sign-in links. Cybersecurity News previously reported fake Exchange Online alerts that used outage claims to lure users into clicking. That campaign has not been linked to the current incident. Update: Microsoft says it has developed a second fix for a remaining issue that prevents some New Outlook users from opening or saving certain types of attachments. We've developed a secondary fix to address the remaining impact when opening/saving specific attachment types. We're performing final validations on this fix before deploying to the affected environment. For more information, see EX1561765 in the admin center. — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 21, 2026 The company is completing final checks and has not yet deployed the fix to affected users. Administrators can follow the rollout under EX1561765 in the Microsoft 365 admin center. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for SIEM
items.summary: We’re honored that Microsoft has once again been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM). As security environments grow more complex and attackers move faster, organizations need more than the ability to collect and analyze data. They need comprehensive visibility, context to understand what is happening, and the ability to act before an attack causes further damage. Explore Microsoft Sentinel SIEM capabilities Comprehensive SIEM across the digital estate Microsoft Sentinel is our cloud-native SIEM, bringing together security data, advanced analytics, automation, and threat intelligence to help organizations protect their digital estate. With more than 500 connectors across Microsoft and third-party solutions, Microsoft Sentinel brings together signals from across complex, multicloud environments. Its rich library of out-of-the-box detections, informed by Microsoft’s threat intelligence and organizational context, helps defenders identify sophisticated threats without building every detection from scratch. Microsoft Sentinel supports the core capabilities security teams depend on, from scalable security data management and advanced detection to threat hunting, investigation, and response. The Microsoft Sentinel data lake centralizes historical and real-time security data across platforms and clouds for cost-effective retention and advanced analytics at scale. Security operations center (SOC) optimization and cost management help teams improve coverage, identify detection gaps, and make informed decisions about the data they collect and retain. Reimagining security operations for the agentic era On September 23, 2026, Microsoft introduced the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender , reimagining security operations for the agentic era. As threats grow more sophisticated and security environments more complex, traditional approaches built on disconnected tools and workflows can no longer keep pace. ISOC brings security operations and threat protection together, creating a unified foundation where people and AI agents can see, understand, and act across the environment. Through deep integration with Microsoft Sentinel, ISOC combines the full breadth of SIEM capabilities with extended detection and response (XDR), threat intelligence, posture management, and response. By connecting signals from Microsoft and third-party environments with rich security context and coordinated action, ISOC enables security teams to move beyond fragmented investigations toward faster, more proactive protection. Rather than operating as separate tools, the security stack works as one system, providing the foundation for agentic security. Attack disruption demonstrates what this integrated approach makes possible . Microsoft Defender correlates signals across Microsoft and third-party environments with threat intelligence to identify high-confidence attacks in progress and automatically contain compromised users and devices before threats spread. This includes ransomware, business email compromise, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Across customers, ransomware attacks are disrupted in just 30 seconds on average . Together, these capabilities demonstrate how Microsoft is moving security operations beyond detection and response toward an integrated, agentic approach that helps organizations anticipate, investigate, and stop threats faster. A shared foundation for people and agents AI is becoming part of how security teams work every day. Microsoft Sentinel combines advanced analytics, machine learning, and automation to help analysts use natural language to hunt for threats, generate response playbooks, support alert triage, analyze complex signals, and accelerate investigations. These capabilities reduce manual work and give defenders more time to focus on the threats and decisions that matter most. By enabling SIEM and native protection to operate as one system, ISOC gives people and AI agents a shared foundation to see, understand, and act across the environment. Agents bring speed and scale to continuous security operations, while people provide expertise, judgment, and accountability. Together, they can move beyond traditional, linear workflows toward continuous detection, investigation, and attack disruption. As agents take on more security operations workflows, comprehensive data, and rich context, the ability to act becomes even more important to helping organizations stop threats faster and deliver better security outcomes. Looking ahead The future of SIEM is about more than managing security data. It’s about ensuring your SIEM is a core building block of the agentic SOC, bringing together security data, intelligence, AI, and native protection so people and agents can understand threats sooner, act faster, and stop attacks before they spread. We’ll continue investing in the comprehensive SIEM capabilities customers rely on while advancing integrated, agentic security operations in Microsoft Defender. We’re grateful for the Gartner recognition and for the customers, partners, and security community whose feedback continues to shape Microsoft Sentinel. Learn more Explore Microsoft Sentinel . Learn about the Integrated Security Operations Center in Microsoft Defender. To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website . Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn ( Microsoft Security ) and X ( @MSFTSecurity ) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity.

items.title: Over 100 Debian Packages Still Contain Distrusted CA Certificates Despite Security Updates
items.summary: A scan of a Debian package mirror found that more than 100 packages still contained copies of distrusted certificate authority (CA) certificates after Debian removed them from its system trust store. Debian developer Steve McIntyre posted the scan results to the Debian developer mailing list on November 19. The findings show why updating the operating system’s trust store does not necessarily change which certificates an application accepts. On October 20, Debian removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 and Comodo AAA Services root certificates after several eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were compromised. Debian fixed its shared ca-certificates package in version 20250419+deb13u1 for Debian 13 “trixie” and 20250419~deb12u2 for Debian 12 “bookworm.” Unlike a Debian kernel security update , this fix changes which certificate chains applications accept, but only if they use the updated trust store. Distrusted CA Certificates Remained A trust store is a list of certificates an application relies on to verify the identity of a server before making an encrypted connection. Debian provides a shared list through ca-certificates , but some packages ship their own copies. An application that relies on a separate list can still accept a certificate chain that another application on the same machine rejects. This is distinct from the changes covered in our report on shorter Let’s Encrypt TLS certificate lifetimes , which concern when server certificates expire. Debian developer Enrico Zini drew attention to the issue after using custom ClamAV signatures to look for the certificates on systems he had installed. His scan found copies in packages or files tied to pip, Node.js, gRPC, NSS, AWS tools, and Qt WebEngine. McIntyre then widened the search to his local Debian mirror. Some matches were in sample code or older package versions, so the results do not show that every match represents a currently installed application that still trusts either root. Administrators should install the latest ca-certificates update for their release and check which trust store their applications actually use. Start with services that make outbound HTTPS connections and tools that download software or handle cloud credentials. Check containers, Flatpaks, and Python virtual environments separately. Updating the host does not necessarily replace certificate files shipped inside them. Use Debian’s security advisories and package tracker to verify the installed version and follow related updates. McIntyre argued that Debian packages should use the shared system trust store instead of shipping their own. Other developers discussed rebuilding packages or replacing bundled copies with links to the system store where possible. That would let future distrust updates reach more applications through one package. Until then, a file match is a starting point: verify whether the running application loads that file before deciding whether it needs a separate fix. items.title: Critical Ruby String Case-Conversion Vulnerabilities Could Lead to Remote Code Execution
items.summary: Published November 20, 2026. We will update this post as new information becomes available. On November 19, 2026, the Ruby development team disclosed multiple security vulnerabilities affecting the Ruby runtime, including two memory corruption flaws in string case conversion that could potentially allow remote code execution (RCE). The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-132825 (GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5) and GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px , were classified as Critical and High severity, respectively. Security research conducted by OpenAI’s security researchers and the use of OpenAI Codex, demonstrated how these vulnerabilities could be exploited through unauthenticated HTTP requests against Ruby on Rails applications. OpenAI also contributed to exploit validation, coordinated disclosure, and remediation efforts. These findings are particularly concerning because the vulnerabilities reside in Ruby’s core string-handling functionality, potentially exposing applications that process untrusted input through affected conversion paths. Understanding the Vulnerabilities Both vulnerabilities involve memory corruption during Ruby string case conversion. Although they share similarities, they originate from different flaws and require different exploitation techniques. CVE-2026-132825: Heap Buffer Overflow in String Case Conversion (Critical) The first vulnerability is a one-byte heap buffer overflow affecting Ruby’s handling of certain character encodings. When converting strings to uppercase, some characters expand into multiple bytes. For example, the German sharp-s character (ß) can expand into “SS” when processed using encodings such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252. Under vulnerable conditions, Ruby fails to properly account for the additional space required during conversion, resulting in a write beyond the allocated memory buffer. Although the overflow involves only a single byte, memory corruption vulnerabilities of this nature can potentially be exploited to manipulate application execution. Published research demonstrated that the vulnerability can be reached through Rack’s multipart form processing in Ruby on Rails applications. Specifically, the _method parameter, commonly used to override HTTP methods in HTML forms, can provide an unauthenticated entry point to the vulnerable functionality. Researchers successfully demonstrated remote code execution against vulnerable Rails applications without requiring authentication. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px: Integer Overflow in String Case Conversion (High) The second vulnerability involves an integer overflow when Ruby calculates the memory required for case conversion of exceptionally large strings. Certain Unicode characters expand into multiple characters during conversion. When the resulting string exceeds the supported length calculation, an integer overflow can cause Ruby to allocate insufficient memory, potentially resulting in a heap buffer overflow. Unlike the first vulnerability, exploitation requires a more complex sequence of operations and significant memory manipulation. Published research demonstrated an RCE chain involving Rack multipart processing, WebSocket connections, heap manipulation, and memory disclosure. The demonstrated exploit also included techniques to bypass Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), illustrating how a memory corruption issue can potentially be developed into a more sophisticated attack. Why are these vulnerabilities concerning? The primary concern is the demonstrated ability to turn vulnerabilities in Ruby’s internal string handling into remotely exploitable conditions through common web application functionality. Several characteristics make these vulnerabilities particularly significant: Unauthenticated exploitation: Researchers demonstrated RCE without requiring valid credentials or prior access to the application. Framework-level exposure: Vulnerable functionality may be reached through standard request processing, even when application developers do not explicitly invoke Ruby’s affected string conversion methods. Multiple encoding options: The underlying behavior is not limited to a single character or encoding, making detection based solely on specific byte sequences insufficient. Different exploitation techniques: The two vulnerabilities demonstrate distinct paths to memory corruption and code execution, complicating efforts to develop comprehensive network-level mitigations. Beyond a Single Character or Encoding Imperva Threat Research’s analysis identified 103 Unicode characters that expand during case conversion , including 16 that expand from one character to three. These characters can be represented through 41 character sets, including ISO-8859-1, Windows-1252, and ISO-8859-7. This highlights an important challenge for security solutions: detecting a single suspicious character, such as ß, is not sufficient to address every potentially vulnerable conversion path. Effective mitigation requires understanding how character encodings, application request processing, and vulnerable runtime behavior interact. It is important to distinguish the broader set of expansion characters from confirmed exploitability. Not every character or encoding combination necessarily triggers either vulnerability. Severity and Potential Impact Ruby’s official security advisories classify the two vulnerabilities as follows: Vulnerability Severity Potential impact CVE-2026-132825 / GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 Critical Heap buffer overflow, potentially leading to RCE GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px High Integer overflow and heap corruption, potentially leading to RCE Working exploitation research has demonstrated remote code execution in specific environments. However, successful exploitation depends on factors including the affected Ruby version, application framework, memory allocator, and runtime configuration. The existence of working exploitation research does not necessarily mean that all applications using vulnerable Ruby versions are remotely exploitable. Who is affected? Published November 20, 2026. We will update this post as new information becomes available.

On November 19, 2026, the Ruby development team disclosed multiple security vulnerabilities affecting the Ruby runtime, including two memory corruption flaws in string case conversion that could potentially allow remote code execution (RCE).

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-132825 (GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5) and GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, were classified as Critical and High severity, respectively.

Security research conducted by OpenAI’s security researchers and the use of OpenAI Codex, demonstrated how these vulnerabilities could be exploited through unauthenticated HTTP requests against Ruby on Rails applications. OpenAI also contributed to exploit validation, coordinated disclosure, and remediation efforts.

These findings are particularly concerning because the vulnerabilities reside in Ruby’s core string-handling functionality, potentially exposing applications that process untrusted input through affected conversion paths.

Understanding the Vulnerabilities

Both vulnerabilities involve memory corruption during Ruby string case conversion. Although they share similarities, they originate from different flaws and require different exploitation techniques.

CVE-2026-132825: Heap Buffer Overflow in String Case Conversion (Critical)

The first vulnerability is a one-byte heap buffer overflow affecting Ruby’s handling of certain character encodings.

When converting strings to uppercase, some characters expand into multiple bytes. For example, the German sharp-s character (ß) can expand into “SS” when processed using encodings such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252.

Under vulnerable conditions, Ruby fails to properly account for the additional space required during conversion, resulting in a write beyond the allocated memory buffer.

Although the overflow involves only a single byte, memory corruption vulnerabilities of this nature can potentially be exploited to manipulate application execution.

Published research demonstrated that the vulnerability can be reached through Rack’s multipart form processing in Ruby on Rails applications. Specifically, the _method parameter, commonly used to override HTTP methods in HTML forms, can provide an unauthenticated entry point to the vulnerable functionality.

Researchers successfully demonstrated remote code execution against vulnerable Rails applications without requiring authentication.

GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px: Integer Overflow in String Case Conversion (High)

The second vulnerability involves an integer overflow when Ruby calculates the memory required for case conversion of exceptionally large strings.

Certain Unicode characters expand into multiple characters during conversion. When the resulting string exceeds the supported length calculation, an integer overflow can cause Ruby to allocate insufficient memory, potentially resulting in a heap buffer overflow.

Unlike the first vulnerability, exploitation requires a more complex sequence of operations and significant memory manipulation.

Published research demonstrated an RCE chain involving Rack multipart processing, WebSocket connections, heap manipulation, and memory disclosure.

The demonstrated exploit also included techniques to bypass Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), illustrating how a memory corruption issue can potentially be developed into a more sophisticated attack.

Why are these vulnerabilities concerning?

The primary concern is the demonstrated ability to turn vulnerabilities in Ruby’s internal string handling into remotely exploitable conditions through common web application functionality.

Several characteristics make these vulnerabilities particularly significant:

  • Unauthenticated exploitation: Researchers demonstrated RCE without requiring valid credentials or prior access to the application.
  • Framework-level exposure: Vulnerable functionality may be reached through standard request processing, even when application developers do not explicitly invoke Ruby’s affected string conversion methods.
  • Multiple encoding options: The underlying behavior is not limited to a single character or encoding, making detection based solely on specific byte sequences insufficient.
  • Different exploitation techniques: The two vulnerabilities demonstrate distinct paths to memory corruption and code execution, complicating efforts to develop comprehensive network-level mitigations.
Beyond a Single Character or Encoding

Imperva Threat Research’s analysis identified 103 Unicode characters that expand during case conversion, including 16 that expand from one character to three.

These characters can be represented through 41 character sets, including ISO-8859-1, Windows-1252, and ISO-8859-7.

This highlights an important challenge for security solutions: detecting a single suspicious character, such as ß, is not sufficient to address every potentially vulnerable conversion path.

Effective mitigation requires understanding how character encodings, application request processing, and vulnerable runtime behavior interact.

It is important to distinguish the broader set of expansion characters from confirmed exploitability. Not every character or encoding combination necessarily triggers either vulnerability.

Severity and Potential Impact

Ruby’s official security advisories classify the two vulnerabilities as follows:

Vulnerability Severity Potential impact CVE-2026-132825 / GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 Critical Heap buffer overflow, potentially leading to RCE GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px High Integer overflow and heap corruption, potentially leading to RCE

Working exploitation research has demonstrated remote code execution in specific environments.

However, successful exploitation depends on factors including the affected Ruby version, application framework, memory allocator, and runtime configuration.

The existence of working exploitation research does not necessarily mean that all applications using vulnerable Ruby versions are remotely exploitable.

Who is affected?

The vulnerabilities affect the following Ruby versions:

Ruby branch Vulnerable versions Fixed version Ruby 4.0 4.0.0 to 4.0.9 4.0.10 Ruby 3.4 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 3.4.13 Ruby 3.3 Up to 3.3.13 3.3.14

Older unsupported Ruby branches may also contain vulnerable code and should be migrated to supported, patched versions.

Internet-facing Ruby on Rails applications deserve particular attention due to the demonstrated unauthenticated exploitation paths.

Other applications built using Ruby, including Sinatra-based applications and products that bundle their own Ruby runtime, should also be evaluated based on their versions and exposure to untrusted input.

What you should do

Organizations running affected Ruby versions should prioritize the following actions:

  1. Upgrade Ruby immediately. Update to Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10, as appropriate. Updating application dependencies alone does not necessarily remediate vulnerabilities in the Ruby runtime.
  2. Identify vulnerable deployments. Review Ruby installations across application servers, containers, bundled runtimes, and internet-facing services.
  3. Review application exposure. Pay particular attention to applications that process unauthenticated HTTP requests, multipart form submissions, or untrusted strings using affected character encodings.
  4. Monitor suspicious requests. Investigate unusual multipart form submissions, unexpected character encodings, abnormal _method parameters, and exceptionally large HTTP requests.
  5. Maintain defense in depth. Use web application security controls to reduce exposure while ensuring vulnerable runtimes are patched.
How Imperva Protects You

Imperva Threat Research has analyzed the disclosed Ruby vulnerabilities and their exploitation techniques, identifying attack patterns that can be detected and mitigated at the network level.

For Cloud WAF, Imperva for Google Cloud, Imperva for AWS and Elastic WAF, Imperva developed and deployed dedicated mitigation rules to protect customers against exploitation attempts targeting these vulnerabilities. These protections are enabled by default, requiring no additional configuration or action from customers.

For WAF Gateway, manual mitigation steps will be provided as soon as possible and ADC content, will be released early next week.

Our mitigation approach accounts for the unique characteristics of these vulnerabilities, including specially encoded multipart parameters and character conversion patterns that could trigger memory corruption in vulnerable Ruby runtimes.

Imperva Threat Research continues to monitor emerging exploitation techniques and will update protections as needed to address new attack variations.

While these protections provide an important additional layer of security, we strongly recommend upgrading affected Ruby installations to patched versions as the primary remediation.

What’s Next?

Imperva Threat Research continues to investigate these vulnerabilities, including publicly available exploitation techniques and potential attack activity.

We will update this post as new information becomes available and provide additional guidance as appropriate.

items.title: PHP Runtime Vulnerabilities: What You Need To Know
items.summary: Published November 20, 2026. We will update this post as new information becomes available. On November 19, 2026, the PHP development team published security fixes for 17 vulnerabilities affecting supported PHP 8.2, 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5 releases. Seven carry a critical CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. The issues span several parts of the language and its runtime: PHP-FPM, session handling, SOAP, PHAR archives, HTTP and FTP streams, and newer URI and DOM APIs. The most severe issues include flaws that can allow remote code execution, but exposure depends on how an application uses PHP and, in some cases, on particular PHP-FPM or php.ini settings. Other fixes address information disclosure, cross-site scripting (XSS), denial of service (DoS), memory corruption, and a local privilege escalation path. The advisories do not describe one shared attack campaign; they document separate vulnerabilities with distinct prerequisites. Read on to learn about the vulnerabilities, and steps you need to take to protect yourself. Seven critical vulnerabilities The critical advisories include several routes to code execution, along with a PHP-FPM request-smuggling issue: CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS 9.2): PHP-FPM request smuggling . PHP may fail to discard unread request-body bytes before reusing a persistent FastCGI or LSAPI connection. In the PHP-FPM scenario described by the advisory, an unauthenticated attacker can arrange for leftover bytes to be interpreted as another FastCGI request, potentially bypassing front-end routing and executing PHP code with the worker’s privileges. CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS 9.2): timezone-cache use-after-free . Under affected startup and logging conditions, PHP can retain a reference to freed timezone-cache memory. A later diagnostic during early request initialization can trigger memory corruption, a worker crash, and potentially code execution with the PHP worker’s privileges. CVE-2026-126714 (CVSS 9.2): partially overwritten session files . If a write to PHP’s default file-based session store is interrupted, the file can contain pieces of both old and new serialized session data. If an attacker can influence session contents and interrupt the write, a later read may deserialize attacker-controlled objects; remote code execution then depends on a suitable object gadget chain in the application. CVE-2026-115560 (CVSS 9.2): session serializer mismatch . PHP’s session upload-progress feature can write attacker-controlled data in one serialization format and later parse it using another. A suitable application object gadget chain may turn the resulting interpretation into code execution with the worker’s privileges. CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS 9.2): Use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown . This vulnerability affects PHP 8.3 and later and requires specific application behavior, including a fatal error during session cleanup. Exploitation also depends on subsequent requests reaching the same PHP worker, where a stale memory pointer may trigger a use-after-free. CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS 9.2): Use-after-free in magic-method backtraces . This vulnerability affects PHP 8.5 and may lead to remote code execution. However, the demonstrated exploitation path requires specific application behavior and non-default PHP configuration settings, including fatal_error_backtraces=1 and zend.exception_ignore_args=0. Notably, PHP’s production configuration sets the latter to 1, preventing the demonstrated exploitation path. CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS 9.2): Use-after-free in fatal-error backtraces . This vulnerability affects PHP 8.5 and requires a specific combination of configuration mismatches, shutdown-time errors, and subsequent requests reaching the same PHP worker. These conditions make exploitation dependent on particular server configurations and runtime behavior rather than a straightforward malicious HTTP request. Other high-severity issues Four additional vulnerabilities received high-severity ratings, including issues affecting PHAR signature verification, PHP-FPM privilege escalation, and PHP’s network stream wrappers. These vulnerabilities involve server-side operations, local privilege escalation, or outbound network communication rather than attack patterns that can be reliably mitigated through inbound WAF inspection. As such, they fall outside the scope of Imperva Cloud WAF protection. Customers are advised to apply the relevant PHP security updates to address these issues. Fixed versions The PHP project released security updates for the 8.2 through 8.5 branches on November 19: PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. Administrators should identify the PHP runtime and deployment mode in use, then apply the appropriate vendor-supported update. PHP distributions and managed hosting providers may package the fixes on their own schedules, so teams should verify their actual runtime build rather than relying only on an application dependency manifest. PHP 8.6.0 was also announced on November 19. The advisories listed above specify affected version ranges in PHP 8.2 through 8.5; consult the individual advisory and the PHP changelog when assessing a particular build or downstream package. What you should do now Updating PHP is the primary way to address these runtime flaws. A web application firewall can provide an additional layer of protection by inspecting and filtering malicious HTTP requests before they reach exposed application endpoints, including PHP-FPM-backed services. That layer does not replace updating the PHP runtime, and it cannot address every condition described in these advisories, including vulnerable outbound stream handling, local PHP-FPM master-process paths, or flaws that depend on application behavior and server configuration. How Imperva Protects You Imperva provides a set of protections against several of the recently disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. Cloud WAF, Imperva for Google Cloud, Imperva for AWS and Elastic WAF, provide mitigation for these vulnerabilities, as detailed in the protection status below. For WAF-GW, manual mitigation steps will be provided as soon as possible and ADC content, will be released early next week. Protection is not enabled by default. Please contact the support team to enable it in your account. Protection Status CVE Protection Status Details CVE-2026-129289 Protected out of the box Existing protections mitigate the identified attack vector. We continue strengthening detection across additional variants. CVE-2026-129496 Opt-in protection available A dedicated security rule is available for customers to enable. Protection is not enabled by default . CVE-2026-126714 Protected out of the box Existing security protections mitigate the identified attack vector. CVE-2026-115560 Protected out of the box Existing security protections mitigate the identified attack vector. CVE-2026-129481 Limited exploitability Exploitation requires complex, application-specific conditions and particular PHP runtime behavior. CVE-2026-129182 Limited exploitability Exploitation requires specific PHP configuration mismatches and runtime conditions. CVE-2026-129474 Limited exploitability Imperva is evaluating exploitability and potential WAF mitigation opportunities. Imperva WAF solutions help protect web applications from malicious HTTP traffic and can reduce exposure to request-based exploit attempts. Organizations should continue to patch PHP and review configuration-dependent exposure as fixes become available from their PHP distribution or hosting provider.

items.title: 3 High-Value Use Cases for Integrating Fidelis Network With Prisma Access
items.summary: Key Takeaways Integrating Fidelis Network with Prisma Access enables deeper inspection of replicated network traffic beyond initial access control decisions. Fidelis Network uses its DLP and threat detection capabilities to identify potentially suspicious transfers of sensitive data, PII, and intellectual property. Packet captures, session-level metadata, alerts, and asset information help analysts investigate suspicious activity and assess potentially affected systems. Analysis of replicated traffic helps security teams investigate potentially malicious communications and assess activity against known adversary techniques aligned with MITRE ATT&CK. Organizations must configure traffic replication and SSL decryption policies, GCP storage and access, network connectivity, and compatible software versions to support effective traffic analysis. Securing access to enterprise resources is an important first step, but it does not provide all the visibility needed to investigate suspicious network activity. Even when access is authorized, security teams may need to determine whether sensitive data is being transferred outside the organization, malicious communications are occurring, or a session involves compromised systems. Prisma Access secures connectivity and network traffic for mobile users and remote networks. By integrating Fidelis Network ® , organizations can analyze replicated network traffic to apply additional threat detection capabilities, identify potentially suspicious data transfers or malicious communications, and access packet-level evidence to investigate suspicious sessions. This complementary analysis provides security teams with greater visibility into network activity, session-level context, and forensic evidence to support threat investigation and incident response. Prisma Access traffic replication, combined with Fidelis Network’s network visibility, threat detection, data loss prevention (DLP) and forensic investigation capabilities enables organizations to analyze replicated traffic for potential data exfiltration, investigate suspicious sessions, and detect advanced malware activity. The integration helps with three high-value scenarios, including data protection, network forensics, and malware detection and response. How the Fidelis Network and Prisma Access Integration Works The integration leverages Prisma Access traffic replication to enable Fidelis Network to access packet capture (PCAP) data, which it can then analyze. Fidelis Network analyzes replicated packet captures from configured Prisma Access locations, enabling security teams to examine available network traffic for signs of suspicious activity and gather additional evidence to support investigation. This visibility is limited to the traffic replicated and made available for analysis. The integration workflow involves several components: Prisma Access: Replicates network traffic for configured mobile user and remote network locations. PCAP storage: Stores encrypted packet capture files in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) storage buckets. Fidelis PCAP Fetcher: Retrieves the replicated PCAP files and transfers them to a designated Fidelis storage bucket. Fidelis Network Sensor: Processes the files, decrypts them using the required private key, and replays the traffic for analysis. Fidelis Command Post and Collector: Receive relevant alerts and asset information, while the Collector receives session metadata to support investigation and analysis. Integrating the Fidelis Network with Palo Alto PRISMA Access How the integration works Things to keep in mind before you begin What it looks like once integrated Read the Guide When SSL decryption is enabled for packet captures, Prisma Access applies the configured decryption policies. Only traffic matching the applicable inline SSL decryption policy is decrypted. Fidelis Network ® then analyzes the available traffic and generates relevant alerts based on its detection capabilities. This workflow provides security teams with additional visibility into network activity and supports the following use cases. Use Case 1: Detecting Data Exfiltration and Protecting Sensitive Information Valuable data may be leaking from an organisation via a seemingly legitimate network session. For instance, an authorized account can be utilized to move personally identifiable information (PII), trade confidential company information, or intellectual property to an unauthorized location. The access control events may not be sufficient in themselves to distinguish whether such events are security related or not. By integrating Fidelis Network with Prisma Access, security teams can examine copies of network traffic for possible data loss, data exfiltration , and other threats. How the integration helps Prisma Access copies the traffic from configured locations and provides the PCAP files for analysis by Fidelis Network. Once the files have been processed, Fidelis Network can review network content available, and utilize its DLP and threat detection features to determine if there are any suspicious transfers. This helps security teams investigate questions such as: Is sensitive information being transferred outside the organization? Does a network session contain PII or intellectual property that requires investigation? Is an observed transfer consistent with expected business activity, or does it warrant further scrutiny? Analysts can view content in the network available through a variety of protocols and ports that may not be visible from the access or connection level. Business value This use case provides organizations the opportunity to explore possible data exposures, while enhancing their capacity to detect suspicious information transfers. This will help security teams prioritize investigations and decide if more containment or remediation is needed, based on the resulting alerts and session context. This extra visibility can assist with enhanced data protection and incident response within enterprises that process sensitive customer data, financial records, or proprietary IP. Use Case 2: Improving Network Forensics and Incident Investigation The first step in an investigation is to determine whether or not there has been a security incident that is suspicious. Analysts may require information on what happened in the session, what systems were used, what did happen on the network, and whether there are related events showing that the network is being compromised. If there is not enough evidence in the session, investigations may be protracted and leave security teams with a lack of understanding into the incident. By integrating with Prisma Access, Fidelis Network enables more thorough network forensics because of the ability to provide replicated packet captures for more in-depth analysis. How the integration helps Replicated traffic is stored as encrypted PCAP files in Prisma Access. These files are retrieved by the Fidelis PCAP Fetcher and then analyzed and replayed by the Fidelis Network Sensor’s traffic analyzer. Fidelis Network is responsible for analyzing the replayed traffic, creating alerts as necessary, gathering asset data, and transferring session metadata to the Collector during analysis. Relevant alerts and assets on the Command Post are provided to aid security monitoring and investigation. This workflow provides analysts with extra network elements they can use to assist in investigating suspicious sessions. For instance, if an alert is generated for potentially malicious traffic, analysts can review the traffic and metadata to get a better understanding of the session. They can match the evidence available with asset data and other security information to conduct an investigation of the extent of the incident. Business value Access to session-level metadata and replicated network traffic can help security teams: Reconstruct suspicious network activity using available packet-level evidence. Investigate the context surrounding a security alert. Identify potentially affected assets and examine related activity. Support historical detection and follow-up investigations using collected metadata. This is especially useful for businesses that must explore intricate incidents throughout distributed users and far-flung network locations. Analysts don’t just have to take the word of an initial alert, but they can take advantage of greater network evidence to help inform a better assessment of incidents. Use Case 3: Detecting Advanced Malware and Supporting Response The possibility for malware activity exists in network sessions that are authorized by existing access policies. Compromised endpoint or account can transmit to suspicious sites, send malicious files, or be involved in activity linked to a larger attack. A security team needs to look at network activity and evidence after they make a connection decision. By integrating with Prisma Access, the Fidelis Network can be used to analyze replicated network traffic for advanced malware detection and investigation. How the integration helps Prisma Access traffic replication supplies the packet captures used by Fidelis Network for analysis. The Fidelis Network Sensor processes the captures and replays the traffic through its analyzer, where relevant security events can trigger alerts to the Command Post. Fidelis Network’s detection capabilities support malware analysis across the attack lifecycle, including detection methods aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK framework . This helps security teams examine suspicious activity in the context of known adversary techniques. For example, if a replicated session contains traffic associated with potentially malicious communication, security analysts can investigate the available packet data, alerts, and asset information to determine whether the activity warrants further response. The integration also provides session-level metadata that can support additional investigation and historical analysis. Business value This use case strengthens the evidence available to security teams when investigating potential malware incidents. Analysts can use network traffic, relevant alerts, and asset context to investigate suspicious behavior and determine appropriate response actions. Combining access security with deeper traffic analysis helps organizations investigate threats that may not be fully understood through access decisions alone. It also supports a more informed approach to incident prioritization and response. Key Benefits of Integrating Fidelis Network With Prisma Access Across these three use cases, the integration provides several security benefits. Deeper network visibility Security teams gain visibility into available network content from replicated traffic, including inbound and outbound sessions across ports and protocols. Where applicable decryption policies permit it, decrypted traffic can provide additional evidence for investigation. Automated threat detection and alerting Fidelis Network analyzes replayed traffic and generates relevant alerts, helping security teams identify activity that requires further investigation. Improved forensic investigation Session-level metadata collection and storage support historical detection and investigation. Analysts can use this information alongside packet-level evidence and asset context to investigate suspicious activity. Better understanding of the enterprise environment Fidelis Network provides a contextual view of the organization’s cyber terrain, helping security teams understand assets and investigate potential threats in their environment. Support for malware analysis across the attack lifecycle Detection methods aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK framework help analysts assess potentially malicious activity in the context of known attack techniques. Implementation Considerations Organizations planning this integration should account for the infrastructure, access controls, and configuration requirements described in the integration guide. The documented architecture uses GCP for the PCAP Fetcher, Fidelis Network Sensor , and packet capture storage. It also requires a GCP service account with read-only access to the relevant Prisma Access storage buckets, along with the appropriate certificate and private key for processing encrypted captures. Organizations should also consider the following: Traffic replication scope: Configure the mobile user or remote network locations for which traffic replication is required. items.summary_html:
Key Takeaways
  • Integrating Fidelis Network with Prisma Access enables deeper inspection of replicated network traffic beyond initial access control decisions.
  • Fidelis Network uses its DLP and threat detection capabilities to identify potentially suspicious transfers of sensitive data, PII, and intellectual property.
  • Packet captures, session-level metadata, alerts, and asset information help analysts investigate suspicious activity and assess potentially affected systems.
  • Analysis of replicated traffic helps security teams investigate potentially malicious communications and assess activity against known adversary techniques aligned with MITRE ATT&CK.
  • Organizations must configure traffic replication and SSL decryption policies, GCP storage and access, network connectivity, and compatible software versions to support effective traffic analysis.

Securing access to enterprise resources is an important first step, but it does not provide all the visibility needed to investigate suspicious network activity. Even when access is authorized, security teams may need to determine whether sensitive data is being transferred outside the organization, malicious communications are occurring, or a session involves compromised systems.

Prisma Access secures connectivity and network traffic for mobile users and remote networks. By integrating Fidelis Network®, organizations can analyze replicated network traffic to apply additional threat detection capabilities, identify potentially suspicious data transfers or malicious communications, and access packet-level evidence to investigate suspicious sessions. This complementary analysis provides security teams with greater visibility into network activity, session-level context, and forensic evidence to support threat investigation and incident response.

Prisma Access traffic replication, combined with Fidelis Network’s network visibility, threat detection, data loss prevention (DLP) and forensic investigation capabilities enables organizations to analyze replicated traffic for potential data exfiltration, investigate suspicious sessions, and detect advanced malware activity.

The integration helps with three high-value scenarios, including data protection, network forensics, and malware detection and response.

How the Fidelis Network and Prisma Access Integration Works

The integration leverages Prisma Access traffic replication to enable Fidelis Network to access packet capture (PCAP) data, which it can then analyze. Fidelis Network analyzes replicated packet captures from configured Prisma Access locations, enabling security teams to examine available network traffic for signs of suspicious activity and gather additional evidence to support investigation. This visibility is limited to the traffic replicated and made available for analysis.

The integration workflow involves several components:

  • Prisma Access: Replicates network traffic for configured mobile user and remote network locations.
  • PCAP storage: Stores encrypted packet capture files in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) storage buckets.
  • Fidelis PCAP Fetcher: Retrieves the replicated PCAP files and transfers them to a designated Fidelis storage bucket.
  • Fidelis Network Sensor: Processes the files, decrypts them using the required private key, and replays the traffic for analysis.
  • Fidelis Command Post and Collector: Receive relevant alerts and asset information, while the Collector receives session metadata to support investigation and analysis.
Integrating the Fidelis Network with Palo Alto PRISMA Access
