  • What it looks like once integrated
Read the Guide

When SSL decryption is enabled for packet captures, Prisma Access applies the configured decryption policies. Only traffic matching the applicable inline SSL decryption policy is decrypted. Fidelis Network® then analyzes the available traffic and generates relevant alerts based on its detection capabilities.

This workflow provides security teams with additional visibility into network activity and supports the following use cases.

Use Case 1: Detecting Data Exfiltration and Protecting Sensitive Information

Valuable data may be leaking from an organisation via a seemingly legitimate network session. For instance, an authorized account can be utilized to move personally identifiable information (PII), trade confidential company information, or intellectual property to an unauthorized location. The access control events may not be sufficient in themselves to distinguish whether such events are security related or not.

By integrating Fidelis Network with Prisma Access, security teams can examine copies of network traffic for possible data loss, data exfiltration, and other threats.

How the integration helps

Prisma Access copies the traffic from configured locations and provides the PCAP files for analysis by Fidelis Network. Once the files have been processed, Fidelis Network can review network content available, and utilize its DLP and threat detection features to determine if there are any suspicious transfers.

This helps security teams investigate questions such as:

  • Is sensitive information being transferred outside the organization?
  • Does a network session contain PII or intellectual property that requires investigation?
  • Is an observed transfer consistent with expected business activity, or does it warrant further scrutiny?

Analysts can view content in the network available through a variety of protocols and ports that may not be visible from the access or connection level.

Business value

This use case provides organizations the opportunity to explore possible data exposures, while enhancing their capacity to detect suspicious information transfers. This will help security teams prioritize investigations and decide if more containment or remediation is needed, based on the resulting alerts and session context.

This extra visibility can assist with enhanced data protection and incident response within enterprises that process sensitive customer data, financial records, or proprietary IP.

Use Case 2: Improving Network Forensics and Incident Investigation

The first step in an investigation is to determine whether or not there has been a security incident that is suspicious. Analysts may require information on what happened in the session, what systems were used, what did happen on the network, and whether there are related events showing that the network is being compromised.

If there is not enough evidence in the session, investigations may be protracted and leave security teams with a lack of understanding into the incident.

By integrating with Prisma Access, Fidelis Network enables more thorough network forensics because of the ability to provide replicated packet captures for more in-depth analysis.

How the integration helps

Replicated traffic is stored as encrypted PCAP files in Prisma Access. These files are retrieved by the Fidelis PCAP Fetcher and then analyzed and replayed by the Fidelis Network Sensor’s traffic analyzer.

Fidelis Network is responsible for analyzing the replayed traffic, creating alerts as necessary, gathering asset data, and transferring session metadata to the Collector during analysis. Relevant alerts and assets on the Command Post are provided to aid security monitoring and investigation.

This workflow provides analysts with extra network elements they can use to assist in investigating suspicious sessions.

For instance, if an alert is generated for potentially malicious traffic, analysts can review the traffic and metadata to get a better understanding of the session. They can match the evidence available with asset data and other security information to conduct an investigation of the extent of the incident.

Business value

Access to session-level metadata and replicated network traffic can help security teams:

  • Reconstruct suspicious network activity using available packet-level evidence.
  • Investigate the context surrounding a security alert.
  • Identify potentially affected assets and examine related activity.
  • Support historical detection and follow-up investigations using collected metadata.

This is especially useful for businesses that must explore intricate incidents throughout distributed users and far-flung network locations. Analysts don’t just have to take the word of an initial alert, but they can take advantage of greater network evidence to help inform a better assessment of incidents.

Use Case 3: Detecting Advanced Malware and Supporting Response

The possibility for malware activity exists in network sessions that are authorized by existing access policies. Compromised endpoint or account can transmit to suspicious sites, send malicious files, or be involved in activity linked to a larger attack.

A security team needs to look at network activity and evidence after they make a connection decision.

By integrating with Prisma Access, the Fidelis Network can be used to analyze replicated network traffic for advanced malware detection and investigation.

How the integration helps

Prisma Access traffic replication supplies the packet captures used by Fidelis Network for analysis. The Fidelis Network Sensor processes the captures and replays the traffic through its analyzer, where relevant security events can trigger alerts to the Command Post.

Fidelis Network’s detection capabilities support malware analysis across the attack lifecycle, including detection methods aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK framework. This helps security teams examine suspicious activity in the context of known adversary techniques.

For example, if a replicated session contains traffic associated with potentially malicious communication, security analysts can investigate the available packet data, alerts, and asset information to determine whether the activity warrants further response.

The integration also provides session-level metadata that can support additional investigation and historical analysis.

Business value

This use case strengthens the evidence available to security teams when investigating potential malware incidents. Analysts can use network traffic, relevant alerts, and asset context to investigate suspicious behavior and determine appropriate response actions.

Combining access security with deeper traffic analysis helps organizations investigate threats that may not be fully understood through access decisions alone. It also supports a more informed approach to incident prioritization and response.

Key Benefits of Integrating Fidelis Network With Prisma Access

Across these three use cases, the integration provides several security benefits.

Deeper network visibility

Security teams gain visibility into available network content from replicated traffic, including inbound and outbound sessions across ports and protocols. Where applicable decryption policies permit it, decrypted traffic can provide additional evidence for investigation.

Automated threat detection and alerting

Fidelis Network analyzes replayed traffic and generates relevant alerts, helping security teams identify activity that requires further investigation.

Improved forensic investigation

Session-level metadata collection and storage support historical detection and investigation. Analysts can use this information alongside packet-level evidence and asset context to investigate suspicious activity.

Better understanding of the enterprise environment

Fidelis Network provides a contextual view of the organization’s cyber terrain, helping security teams understand assets and investigate potential threats in their environment.

Support for malware analysis across the attack lifecycle

Detection methods aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK framework help analysts assess potentially malicious activity in the context of known attack techniques.

Implementation Considerations

Organizations planning this integration should account for the infrastructure, access controls, and configuration requirements described in the integration guide.

The documented architecture uses GCP for the PCAP Fetcher, Fidelis Network Sensor, and packet capture storage. It also requires a GCP service account with read-only access to the relevant Prisma Access storage buckets, along with the appropriate certificate and private key for processing encrypted captures.

Organizations should also consider the following:

  • Traffic replication scope: Configure the mobile user or remote network locations for which traffic replication is required.
  • SSL decryption policies: Confirm that the configured policies support the intended inspection requirements. Only traffic matching the applicable inline SSL decryption policy will be decrypted when the option is enabled.
  • Storage and retention: Prisma Access PCAP files are available for download for up to 72 hours before permanent deletion. The documented maximum capture size is 200 MB or five minutes of packet capture, whichever is smaller.
  • Network connectivity: Establish connectivity between the Fidelis Network Sensor and Command Post using the supported static IP or VPN tunnel approach.
  • Version compatibility: The integration guide documents testing with Prisma Access version 5.2.2 and Fidelis Network version 9.8.x. Organizations should validate their intended deployment configuration and conduct a pilot before production deployment, particularly when using configurations outside the documented scope.

These considerations help teams plan the integration and ensure that traffic replication, processing, and analysis align with their security requirements.

  • Detect encrypted and evasive activity
  • Automate responses with precision

Conclusion

Securing enterprise access is only one part of protecting an organization’s network. Security teams also need the visibility and evidence required to investigate suspicious sessions, detect potential data exfiltration, and respond to malware activity.

Integrating Fidelis Network with Prisma Access extends security analysis beyond the initial access decision by making replicated network traffic available for deeper inspection. The combination supports three important security use cases: DLP and sensitive data exfiltration detection, detailed network forensics, and advanced malware detection and response.

For enterprises managing mobile users and remote networks, this integration can provide additional network context, relevant security alerts, and session-level evidence to support investigation. By bringing traffic replication and network analysis together, organizations can strengthen their ability to understand suspicious activity and make more informed security response decisions.

items.title: Critical Apache Tomcat Flaw Lets Remote Attackers Join Trusted Server Clusters Without Authentication
items.summary: The Apache Software Foundation has disclosed a critical flaw in Apache Tomcat that allows a remote attacker to join a trusted server cluster without authentication. Tracked as CVE-2026-133325, the flaw affects clusters that use TLS 1.3 with a pre-shared key. Apache published the advisory on November 19, 2026, and credited researcher Mike Read with finding the issue. The Apache Tomcat 11 security advisory identifies versions 11.0.28 and 11.0.29 as affected. Apache also lists Tomcat 10.1.62 and 9.0.124. Running one of those versions does not by itself mean a server is exposed. The flaw requires the affected cluster encryption setup, and a remote attacker needs network access to the service that handles communication between cluster members. A public Tomcat website does not necessarily expose that service. Apache Tomcat branch Affected versions Patched version (pending release) 11.0.x 11.0.28–11.0.29 11.0.30 10.1.x 10.1.62 10.1.63 9.0.x 9.0.124 9.0.125 Tomcat Cluster Authentication Failed Apache Tribes handles communication between servers in a Tomcat cluster. Those servers can share session data so that a user can stay signed in when another server takes over. A pre-shared key is a secret configured on trusted members in advance. In the affected TLS 1.3 setup, Tomcat did not verify the identity of the server at the other end of the connection. The connection could be encrypted without proving that the server was allowed to join. Cyber Security News previously covered flaws in Tomcat’s EncryptInterceptor , an older component used to protect cluster traffic. The new advisory concerns a different failure: Tomcat accepted a cluster member it had not authenticated. Apache’s advisory does not report active exploitation or say that joining a cluster gives an attacker remote code execution. Apache recommends switching cluster communication to TLS 1.2 while keeping the pre-shared key enabled. This change applies to traffic between Tomcat servers, not the HTTPS connections used by website visitors. The fixed versions are 11.0.30, 10.1.63, and 9.0.125 for their respective branches. Apache listed them as pending release in its Tomcat 11 , Tomcat 10 , and Tomcat 9 security notices. Administrators should check the running version and cluster settings on every member, restrict cluster ports to approved servers, and review available logs for unexpected membership changes. After applying the workaround or updating, confirm that every expected member reconnects and that session replication still works where enabled. A website can still respond while its servers are no longer sharing session data. The earlier CISA warning about an exploited Tomcat encryption flaw concerned CVE-2026-34486. That warning does not establish exploitation of CVE-2026-133325, and the two flaws should be tracked separately.

items.title: CVE-2026-123890: Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day Exploited by China-Linked Hackers
items.summary: Broadcom has released emergency security updates addressing CVE-2026-123890, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in VMware vCenter Server that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyberespionage actor. The flaw resides in the VMware Directory Service and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical . Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant attributed observed exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE , formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also known as Warp Panda. Forensic evidence indicates that the group exploited the vulnerability in early September 2026, more than two months before Broadcom publicly disclosed and patched it on November 19. The attackers used a custom Golang exploitation utility named BONESAW to target VMware vCenter. Successful exploitation enabled the threat actor to establish an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local, extract the vCenter Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), obtain SAML signing material, create rogue SSO administrator accounts, and execute commands on the affected appliance. Contact Sales The vulnerability is particularly dangerous because vCenter functions as the centralized control plane for VMware virtual infrastructure. Compromise can provide attackers with privileged access not only to the management appliance but potentially to managed ESXi hosts and virtual machines. In the observed intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE eventually accessed an ESXi host and extracted files from a Windows guest VM. Organizations can strengthen defenses against emerging vulnerabilities with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, helping security teams operationalize threat intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to transform emerging vulnerability intelligence into detection logic, generate hunting queries, and adapt behavioral detections to their organization’s available telemetry. Detect CVE-2026-123890 by monitoring access to vCenter management services, especially TCP port 2012, alongside suspicious SSO account creation, unexpected administrative sessions, unusual use of the VAMI API, changes to SSH settings, and abnormal file or database access originating from vCenter. CVE-2026-123890 analysis CVE-2026-123890 affects VMware vCenter Server and related VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and Telco Cloud environments. Broadcom classifies the issue as an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service and assigns it the maximum Critical rating of 9.8 under CVSS 3.1. Mandiant’s technical analysis provides considerably more detail about the underlying weakness. The vulnerability is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session-key disclosure issue reachable through Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC) handled by the vCenter Directory Service, or vmdird. The relevant interface is exposed over TCP port 2012 , which vCenter uses as a control interface for Single Sign-On functionality. ARMORY CASTLE specifically scanned internal environments for VMware-related services on ports including 443, 2012, 5480, and 9080 before exploiting vCenter. The flaw involves VMware’s rpc_srp_verifier service. According to GTIG, weaknesses in cryptographic logic and authorization can expose a shared SRP session key. An attacker can then use this information to establish an authenticated session as: administrator@vsphere.local No valid administrator password is required. Once the authenticated session is established, the attacker can interact with privileged VMware Directory Service interfaces. Mandiant states that an attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the underlying data.mdb database through the vmdirdbcp RPC interface. BONESAW significantly automated these capabilities. Mandiant observed the tool being used to: create a new SSO administrator account; remotely retrieve and parse the vCenter LMDB; extract the VMware Security Token Service private SAML signing key; create a backdoor machine account through vmdir; forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertions; assign Global Administrator privileges through the vSphere SOAP API. This enables attackers to move beyond an initial authentication bypass toward persistent control of the virtualization management layer. The flaw is distinct from CVE-2026-59309, another vCenter authentication bypass disclosed in July 2026. Both issues can ultimately expose a shared session key without knowledge of the user’s password, but they target different interfaces. CVE-2026-59309 involves malformed authorization tokens sent to vmdir over LDAP, while the newer vulnerability abuses the DCE/RPC SRP authentication path. This distinction matters operationally. Mandiant observed BONESAW being executed against a vCenter instance that had already been patched for CVE-2026-59309, demonstrating that fixing the earlier vulnerability does not protect against the newly disclosed weakness. The observed compromise began through a separate zero-day. ARMORY CASTLE initially exploited CVE-2026-102764 in BeyondTrust Remote Support, then moved laterally to internal Linux appliances that lacked EDR coverage. From those hosts, the attackers performed VMware-focused reconnaissance before deploying BONESAW against vCenter. The group used several additional custom malware families during the intrusion, including the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, BEARBONES backdoor, SAWSNAKE SAML utility, and LAZYBONES backdoor. This tooling illustrates the broader post-exploitation ecosystem surrounding the zero-day rather than representing prerequisites for exploitation itself. After compromising vCenter, ARMORY CASTLE used another utility, SAWSNAKE , capable of extracting identity provider signing keys and supporting Golden SAML-style attacks. Forged SAML authentication tokens can allow an attacker to impersonate users and potentially bypass MFA controls. The attackers also enabled SSH on the vCenter appliance through its management API, stole the vCenter master symmetric encryption key and PostgreSQL database credentials, and then disabled SSH again. This highlights why defenders must inspect historical configuration changes rather than checking only the appliance’s current state. The group ultimately moved to an ESXi host, added an SSH public key to the root account, and used VMware filesystem tooling to access virtual-disk contents. Mandiant observed extraction of sensitive Windows files from a guest VM, including registry hive material. A working exploitation tool clearly exists because Mandiant recovered and analyzed BONESAW from real-world attacks. However, GTIG has not released BONESAW, and Censys reported after disclosure that it had not identified publicly available exploit code for this specific vulnerability. Public exploit material for the earlier CVE-2026-59309 should not be confused with an exploit for this new issue. Mandiant recovered BONESAW with a Go build metadata timestamp of July 13, 2026, which predates public disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 by 16 days. Researchers caution that Go build metadata can be modified, so this timestamp alone does not establish when the vulnerability was discovered. Nevertheless, Mandiant says it has evidence ARMORY CASTLE possessed knowledge of the new flaw before the July disclosure of the earlier vCenter vulnerability. For CVE-2026-123890 detection, defenders should prioritize network and identity activity related to vCenter’s control plane. Scanning or unusual connections involving TCP port 2012 are particularly relevant when combined with access to ports 443, 389, 5480, or 9080. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE explicitly scanning these VMware-related services before exploitation. Organizations should also investigate: unexpected SSO administrator accounts; administrative sessions involving administrator@vsphere.local; unexpected access to /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb; VAMI API activity enabling or disabling SSH; new SSH keys added to ESXi root accounts; unexpected extraction of STS or identity-provider signing material; unusual vCenter-to-ESXi lateral movement; unexpected access to virtual disk files. The published CVE-2026-123890 IOCs associated with the broader ARMORY CASTLE intrusion include the BONESAW filename /tmp/123, SAWSNAKE at /tmp/sss, BEARBONES at /tmp/dbr, and LAZYBONES at /usr/bin/vmtoolscs. GTIG also published several suspected obfuscation-network IP addresses, including 103.147.251[.]5, 103.190.38[.]3, 176.9.89[.]66, and 185.71.15[.]109. These indicators should support retrospective hunting but should not be treated as complete evidence of exposure. The vulnerability itself can be exploited without those specific files or infrastructure, and future attackers are unlikely to reuse ARMORY CASTLE’s exact tooling. Security teams seeking additional details for CVE-2026-123890 should distinguish Broadcom’s confirmed vulnerability information from Mandiant’s campaign observations. Broadcom confirms the critical authentication bypass and affected versions, while GTIG/Mandiant provide the evidence for real-world zero-day exploitation, BONESAW capabilities, and ARMORY CASTLE attribution. CVE-2026-123890 Mitigation Broadcom states that there is no workaround for this vulnerability. Organizations running affected VMware environments should therefore install the appropriate patched release as soon as possible. The main fixed versions are: Product / Branch Fixed Version VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation vCenter 9.1.x 9.1.1.0200 VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation vCenter 9.0.x 9.0.2.0200 VMware vCenter Server 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x 5.2.5 VMware vCenter Server 7.0 Contact Broadcom Support with an extended-support contract VMware Telco Cloud Platform / Infrastructure Follow Broadcom KB463116 Broadcom’s advisory explicitly lists VMware vCenter 7.0 as affected but does not provide a generally available fixed release because the branch has reached end of general support. Customers with extended support should contact Broadcom for remediation guidance. Because exploitation occurred before public disclosure, organizations should not treat patch installation as the end of incident response. Any vCenter instance that was reachable by potentially compromised internal hosts while vulnerable should be reviewed for signs of previous compromise. Security teams should examine SSO and directory records for unauthorized accounts, particularly newly created administrators or machine accounts. Accounts that cannot be tied to a legitimate administrative workflow should be treated as suspicious. Defenders should also review vCenter management telemetry for historical SSH enablement. ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH through the appliance management API, collected sensitive information, and disabled it again, meaning a currently disabled SSH service does not prove it was never used maliciously. Check ESXi hosts managed by potentially compromised vCenter instances for unauthorized entries in root authorized_keys, unusual SSH access, unexpected files, or evidence that virtual machine disks were mounted and accessed outside normal administrative workflows. If vCenter compromise is confirmed or strongly suspected, organizations should consider SAML and cryptographic material exposed. This includes STS signing keys, identity-provider certificates, master encryption keys, database credentials, and privileged VMware credentials. Where signing keys may have been stolen, simply changing user passwords may be insufficient because an attacker with the private SAML signing key could forge valid authentication assertions. Incident response should therefore include appropriate certificate and signing-key rotation according to VMware guidance. Network architecture should also be hardened after patching. Mandiant recommends treating the vCenter appliance as a high-value control-plane system and restricting administrative access using Zero Trust principles rather than assuming internal network placement provides adequate protection. Access to sensitive interfaces such as TCP 2012, VAMI on TCP 5480, SSH on TCP 22, and the vSphere API should be restricted to explicitly authorized management systems. Mandiant notes that the default VCSA firewall provides limited port-level granularity and forensic visibility, so additional network controls may be necessary. Organizations should also ensure EDR and centralized logging cover Linux-based infrastructure appliances wherever possible. In the documented campaign, ARMORY CASTLE deliberately moved through internal Linux systems lacking endpoint monitoring before attacking vCenter. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. FAQ What is CVE-2026-123890 and how does it work? CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in VMware vCenter’s Directory Service. The flaw exposes an SRP-6a session key through the vmdird DCE/RPC interface on TCP port 2012. An unauthenticated attacker with network access can use the exposed session information to establish an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local, providing highly privileged access to vCenter. When was CVE-2026-123890 first discovered? The precise date when the vulnerability was initially discovered is not publicly documented. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE exploiting it in early September 2026, while the recovered BONESAW binary contained a July 13 build timestamp. Researchers caution that this timestamp can be modified and therefore is not definitive evidence of the discovery date. Broadcom publicly disclosed the flaw and released fixes on November 19, 2026. What is the impact of CVE-2026-123890 on systems? Successful exploitation provides an authenticated vCenter administrator session without requiring valid credentials. Attackers can execute commands, steal the VMware Directory Service database, obtain SAML signing material, create persistent SSO administrator accounts, and potentially pivot from vCenter to managed ESXi hosts and guest virtual machines. Mandiant describes BONESAW as capable of achieving full compromise of targeted vCenter 7.x and 8.x appliances. Can CVE-2026-123890 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Systems remain exposed if they run an affected VMware vCenter release and have not received the November security updates. Broadcom lists affected branches across vCenter 7.0, 8.0, 9.0.x, 9.1.x, VMware Cloud Foundation, and several Telco Cloud deployments. Because the flaw was exploited before disclosure, organizations that have already patched should still review previously exposed systems for evidence of compromise. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-123890? Install the fixed vCenter release specified by Broadcom immediately because no workaround is available. After patching, inspect SSO administrator accounts, VMware Directory Service activity, historical SSH enablement, SAML signing material, ESXi root SSH keys, and suspicious access to virtual machine disks. Organizations should also restrict access to vCenter management interfaces and improve centralized logging and endpoint visibility across virtualization infrastructure.

Broadcom has released emergency security updates addressing CVE-2026-123890, a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in VMware vCenter Server that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyberespionage actor. The flaw resides in the VMware Directory Service and carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8, Critical.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant attributed observed exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also known as Warp Panda. Forensic evidence indicates that the group exploited the vulnerability in early September 2026, more than two months before Broadcom publicly disclosed and patched it on November 19.

The attackers used a custom Golang exploitation utility named BONESAW to target VMware vCenter. Successful exploitation enabled the threat actor to establish an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local, extract the vCenter Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), obtain SAML signing material, create rogue SSO administrator accounts, and execute commands on the affected appliance.

Contact Sales

The vulnerability is particularly dangerous because vCenter functions as the centralized control plane for VMware virtual infrastructure. Compromise can provide attackers with privileged access not only to the management appliance but potentially to managed ESXi hosts and virtual machines. In the observed intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE eventually accessed an ESXi host and extracted files from a Windows guest VM.

Organizations can strengthen defenses against emerging vulnerabilities with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, helping security teams operationalize threat intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Security professionals can also use Prime Architect to transform emerging vulnerability intelligence into detection logic, generate hunting queries, and adapt behavioral detections to their organization’s available telemetry.

Detect CVE-2026-123890 by monitoring access to vCenter management services, especially TCP port 2012, alongside suspicious SSO account creation, unexpected administrative sessions, unusual use of the VAMI API, changes to SSH settings, and abnormal file or database access originating from vCenter.

CVE-2026-123890 analysis

CVE-2026-123890 affects VMware vCenter Server and related VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and Telco Cloud environments. Broadcom classifies the issue as an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service and assigns it the maximum Critical rating of 9.8 under CVSS 3.1.

Mandiant’s technical analysis provides considerably more detail about the underlying weakness. The vulnerability is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session-key disclosure issue reachable through Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC) handled by the vCenter Directory Service, or vmdird.

The relevant interface is exposed over TCP port 2012, which vCenter uses as a control interface for Single Sign-On functionality. ARMORY CASTLE specifically scanned internal environments for VMware-related services on ports including 443, 2012, 5480, and 9080 before exploiting vCenter.

The flaw involves VMware’s rpc_srp_verifier service. According to GTIG, weaknesses in cryptographic logic and authorization can expose a shared SRP session key. An attacker can then use this information to establish an authenticated session as:

administrator@vsphere.local

No valid administrator password is required.

Once the authenticated session is established, the attacker can interact with privileged VMware Directory Service interfaces. Mandiant states that an attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the underlying data.mdb database through the vmdirdbcp RPC interface.

BONESAW significantly automated these capabilities. Mandiant observed the tool being used to:

  • create a new SSO administrator account;
  • remotely retrieve and parse the vCenter LMDB;
  • extract the VMware Security Token Service private SAML signing key;
  • create a backdoor machine account through vmdir;
  • forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertions;
  • assign Global Administrator privileges through the vSphere SOAP API.

This enables attackers to move beyond an initial authentication bypass toward persistent control of the virtualization management layer.

The flaw is distinct from CVE-2026-59309, another vCenter authentication bypass disclosed in July 2026. Both issues can ultimately expose a shared session key without knowledge of the user’s password, but they target different interfaces. CVE-2026-59309 involves malformed authorization tokens sent to vmdir over LDAP, while the newer vulnerability abuses the DCE/RPC SRP authentication path.

This distinction matters operationally. Mandiant observed BONESAW being executed against a vCenter instance that had already been patched for CVE-2026-59309, demonstrating that fixing the earlier vulnerability does not protect against the newly disclosed weakness.

The observed compromise began through a separate zero-day. ARMORY CASTLE initially exploited CVE-2026-102764 in BeyondTrust Remote Support, then moved laterally to internal Linux appliances that lacked EDR coverage. From those hosts, the attackers performed VMware-focused reconnaissance before deploying BONESAW against vCenter.

The group used several additional custom malware families during the intrusion, including the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, BEARBONES backdoor, SAWSNAKE SAML utility, and LAZYBONES backdoor. This tooling illustrates the broader post-exploitation ecosystem surrounding the zero-day rather than representing prerequisites for exploitation itself.

After compromising vCenter, ARMORY CASTLE used another utility, SAWSNAKE, capable of extracting identity provider signing keys and supporting Golden SAML-style attacks. Forged SAML authentication tokens can allow an attacker to impersonate users and potentially bypass MFA controls.

The attackers also enabled SSH on the vCenter appliance through its management API, stole the vCenter master symmetric encryption key and PostgreSQL database credentials, and then disabled SSH again. This highlights why defenders must inspect historical configuration changes rather than checking only the appliance’s current state.

The group ultimately moved to an ESXi host, added an SSH public key to the root account, and used VMware filesystem tooling to access virtual-disk contents. Mandiant observed extraction of sensitive Windows files from a guest VM, including registry hive material.

A working exploitation tool clearly exists because Mandiant recovered and analyzed BONESAW from real-world attacks. However, GTIG has not released BONESAW, and Censys reported after disclosure that it had not identified publicly available exploit code for this specific vulnerability. Public exploit material for the earlier CVE-2026-59309 should not be confused with an exploit for this new issue.

Mandiant recovered BONESAW with a Go build metadata timestamp of July 13, 2026, which predates public disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 by 16 days. Researchers caution that Go build metadata can be modified, so this timestamp alone does not establish when the vulnerability was discovered. Nevertheless, Mandiant says it has evidence ARMORY CASTLE possessed knowledge of the new flaw before the July disclosure of the earlier vCenter vulnerability.

For CVE-2026-123890 detection, defenders should prioritize network and identity activity related to vCenter’s control plane. Scanning or unusual connections involving TCP port 2012 are particularly relevant when combined with access to ports 443, 389, 5480, or 9080. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE explicitly scanning these VMware-related services before exploitation.

Organizations should also investigate:

  • unexpected SSO administrator accounts;
  • administrative sessions involving administrator@vsphere.local;
  • unexpected access to /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb;
  • VAMI API activity enabling or disabling SSH;
  • new SSH keys added to ESXi root accounts;
  • unexpected extraction of STS or identity-provider signing material;
  • unusual vCenter-to-ESXi lateral movement;
  • unexpected access to virtual disk files.

The published CVE-2026-123890 IOCs associated with the broader ARMORY CASTLE intrusion include the BONESAW filename /tmp/123, SAWSNAKE at /tmp/sss, BEARBONES at /tmp/dbr, and LAZYBONES at /usr/bin/vmtoolscs. GTIG also published several suspected obfuscation-network IP addresses, including 103.147.251[.]5, 103.190.38[.]3, 176.9.89[.]66, and 185.71.15[.]109.

These indicators should support retrospective hunting but should not be treated as complete evidence of exposure. The vulnerability itself can be exploited without those specific files or infrastructure, and future attackers are unlikely to reuse ARMORY CASTLE’s exact tooling.

Security teams seeking additional details for CVE-2026-123890 should distinguish Broadcom’s confirmed vulnerability information from Mandiant’s campaign observations. Broadcom confirms the critical authentication bypass and affected versions, while GTIG/Mandiant provide the evidence for real-world zero-day exploitation, BONESAW capabilities, and ARMORY CASTLE attribution.

CVE-2026-123890 Mitigation

Broadcom states that there is no workaround for this vulnerability. Organizations running affected VMware environments should therefore install the appropriate patched release as soon as possible.

The main fixed versions are:

Product / BranchFixed VersionVMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation vCenter 9.1.x9.1.1.0200VMware Cloud Foundation / vSphere Foundation vCenter 9.0.x9.0.2.0200VMware vCenter Server 8.08.0 U3mVMware Cloud Foundation 5.x5.2.5VMware vCenter Server 7.0Contact Broadcom Support with an extended-support contractVMware Telco Cloud Platform / InfrastructureFollow Broadcom KB463116

Broadcom’s advisory explicitly lists VMware vCenter 7.0 as affected but does not provide a generally available fixed release because the branch has reached end of general support. Customers with extended support should contact Broadcom for remediation guidance.

Because exploitation occurred before public disclosure, organizations should not treat patch installation as the end of incident response. Any vCenter instance that was reachable by potentially compromised internal hosts while vulnerable should be reviewed for signs of previous compromise.

Security teams should examine SSO and directory records for unauthorized accounts, particularly newly created administrators or machine accounts. Accounts that cannot be tied to a legitimate administrative workflow should be treated as suspicious.

Defenders should also review vCenter management telemetry for historical SSH enablement. ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH through the appliance management API, collected sensitive information, and disabled it again, meaning a currently disabled SSH service does not prove it was never used maliciously.

Check ESXi hosts managed by potentially compromised vCenter instances for unauthorized entries in root authorized_keys, unusual SSH access, unexpected files, or evidence that virtual machine disks were mounted and accessed outside normal administrative workflows.

If vCenter compromise is confirmed or strongly suspected, organizations should consider SAML and cryptographic material exposed. This includes STS signing keys, identity-provider certificates, master encryption keys, database credentials, and privileged VMware credentials.

Where signing keys may have been stolen, simply changing user passwords may be insufficient because an attacker with the private SAML signing key could forge valid authentication assertions. Incident response should therefore include appropriate certificate and signing-key rotation according to VMware guidance.

Network architecture should also be hardened after patching. Mandiant recommends treating the vCenter appliance as a high-value control-plane system and restricting administrative access using Zero Trust principles rather than assuming internal network placement provides adequate protection.

Access to sensitive interfaces such as TCP 2012, VAMI on TCP 5480, SSH on TCP 22, and the vSphere API should be restricted to explicitly authorized management systems. Mandiant notes that the default VCSA firewall provides limited port-level granularity and forensic visibility, so additional network controls may be necessary.

Organizations should also ensure EDR and centralized logging cover Linux-based infrastructure appliances wherever possible. In the documented campaign, ARMORY CASTLE deliberately moved through internal Linux systems lacking endpoint monitoring before attacking vCenter.

Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-123890 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass vulnerability in VMware vCenter’s Directory Service. The flaw exposes an SRP-6a session key through the vmdird DCE/RPC interface on TCP port 2012. An unauthenticated attacker with network access can use the exposed session information to establish an authenticated session as administrator@vsphere.local, providing highly privileged access to vCenter.

When was CVE-2026-123890 first discovered?

The precise date when the vulnerability was initially discovered is not publicly documented. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE exploiting it in early September 2026, while the recovered BONESAW binary contained a July 13 build timestamp. Researchers caution that this timestamp can be modified and therefore is not definitive evidence of the discovery date. Broadcom publicly disclosed the flaw and released fixes on November 19, 2026.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-123890 on systems?

Successful exploitation provides an authenticated vCenter administrator session without requiring valid credentials. Attackers can execute commands, steal the VMware Directory Service database, obtain SAML signing material, create persistent SSO administrator accounts, and potentially pivot from vCenter to managed ESXi hosts and guest virtual machines. Mandiant describes BONESAW as capable of achieving full compromise of targeted vCenter 7.x and 8.x appliances.

Can CVE-2026-123890 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Systems remain exposed if they run an affected VMware vCenter release and have not received the November security updates. Broadcom lists affected branches across vCenter 7.0, 8.0, 9.0.x, 9.1.x, VMware Cloud Foundation, and several Telco Cloud deployments. Because the flaw was exploited before disclosure, organizations that have already patched should still review previously exposed systems for evidence of compromise.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-123890?

Install the fixed vCenter release specified by Broadcom immediately because no workaround is available. After patching, inspect SSO administrator accounts, VMware Directory Service activity, historical SSH enablement, SAML signing material, ESXi root SSH keys, and suspicious access to virtual machine disks. Organizations should also restrict access to vCenter management interfaces and improve centralized logging and endpoint visibility across virtualization infrastructure.



The post CVE-2026-123890: Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day Exploited by China-Linked Hackers appeared first on SOC Prime.

A new US initiative aims to improve the chances of intervening before stolen money disappears—and, perhaps more importantly, before victims send more money. The Threat Disruption Center will connect investigators with participating companies to help pause payments, freeze funds, take down malicious domains, and ban accounts scammers use to approach victims. TRM Labs is providing the investigative technology behind the effort. TRM Labs is an existing blockchain intelligence company that helps financial institutions, crypto businesses, and government agencies detect and investigate crypto-related financial crime and fraud. It has been selected as the center’s primary private-sector partner. The Threat Disruption Center sits within the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Center , which is co-led by the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. It will serve as a shared technology and collaboration resource for a task force that includes more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners. The reason The practical aim is to help investigators sort through victim reports, connect related activity, and identify opportunities to intervene. TRM’s CEO told Bloomberg that the company is looking at how artificial intelligence (AI) can help triage reports in near real time and highlight cases where quick action could return funds to victims. Scammers depend on legitimate services to reach people and move their money: social networks, website hosts, banks, payment providers, and cryptocurrency platforms. Those dependencies also create opportunities to interrupt them. The center is intended to provide a standing channel through which investigators and participating companies can share intelligence in near real time. Depending on the circumstances, a company could then: Pause a victim’s payment Freeze stolen funds Take down a malicious domain Ban a social media account used to approach victims The intended beneficiaries are anyone targeted by scams, cybercrime, and sextortion, not just people who own cryptocurrency. For consumers, the most valuable intervention may be the payment they never make. Cryptocurrency investment scams often unfold over time . A scammer builds trust, introduces an apparently profitable investment opportunity, and encourages the victim to keep adding money. The FBI says some victims identified through its existing Operation Level Up initiative were preparing to sell their homes, liquidate retirement savings, or take out substantial loans. Reaching someone before that next transfer can prevent an already serious loss from becoming much worse. What it’s not Tracing money, freezing it, seizing it, and returning it to a victim are different stages. The announcements describe interventions intended to preserve funds while investigations and legal proceedings continue. It should not be mistaken for a new public-facing recovery service, and it does not guarantee that victims will get their money back. The announced route for reporting a scam remains the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, or IC3. Do not wait for a new initiative to reach you. The FBI recommends: Stop sending money immediately. Do not pay additional “taxes,” “verification charges,” or withdrawal fees demanded by a suspicious investment platform. Report the scam promptly at ic3.gov . Rapid reporting can support recovery efforts and help investigators connect related complaints. Be wary of anyone offering to recover your money for a fee. Recovery services can themselves be scams . Verify unexpected contact from law enforcement independently. The FBI warns that criminals impersonate agents and legitimate anti-fraud operations. Contact your local FBI field office to verify an approach rather than relying on an email’s appearance. items.title: CVE-2026-126714: phpAfterShell PHP Session Flaw Can Lead to Remote Code Execution
items.summary: The PHP development team has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-126714, a critical vulnerability dubbed phpAfterShell that can turn partially overwritten session files into an arbitrary deserialization primitive and potentially remote code execution. The flaw carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, Critical and affects PHP applications using the default file-based session handler. Unlike a vulnerability confined to one CMS or framework, phpAfterShell exists in PHP itself. Applications built with WordPress, Laravel, custom PHP frameworks, or other software can therefore fall within the exposure scope if they run a vulnerable PHP release and store sessions as files. Applications using Redis, databases, or other non-file session handlers are outside this specific defect. The vulnerability stems from how PHP updates existing session files. If an update is interrupted at the right moment, part of the new session data can overwrite the beginning of the file while bytes from the previous session remain at the end. PHP may later interpret this hybrid file as valid session state and deserialize attacker-controlled objects when the application calls session_start(). Successful exploitation requires several conditions, including attacker influence over session data, an interruption at a useful point during the write, and a suitable deserialization path. Depthfirst demonstrated that the primitive could be chained with a separate PHP-native memory-corruption technique to achieve code execution inside the PHP worker process. Contact Sales The issue is especially relevant because PHP’s session upload-progress feature can modify a session while PHP is still parsing an unauthenticated multipart request, before application code begins executing. This can give an attacker a pre-authentication path to manipulate file-backed session state under vulnerable configurations. Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize vulnerability intelligence and accelerate hunting for exploitation behavior across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Detect CVE-2026-126714 by correlating suspicious multipart uploads, abnormal PHP session behavior, repeated worker crashes, and unexpected operating-system activity originating from PHP-FPM, Apache, or other PHP worker processes. CVE-2026-126714 analysis CVE-2026-126714 affects supported PHP branches prior to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13 when applications use file-backed sessions. PHP 8.6.0 was released with the correction included. Older PHP 8.1 and earlier releases are end-of-life and should be migrated to a supported branch rather than relied upon for ongoing security updates. The vulnerability is located in PHP’s default files session save handler: session.save_handler = files PHP stores each session in a file such as: /sess_ When session data changes, PHP serializes the new state and writes it into the existing file. The vulnerable design did not treat this update as a fully atomic transaction. Under the default PHP session serialization format, multiple values are stored consecutively as records consisting of a session key and serialized value. Serialized strings contain explicit length information that tells PHP where a value ends and where parsing should continue. That creates an important exploitation opportunity. Data that is harmless while positioned inside a serialized string can become active syntax when the beginning of the file is replaced with another carefully constructed session prefix. Depthfirst researchers showed that two individually legitimate sessions could therefore be combined into a third valid but attacker-influenced session if the update process stops at the appropriate moment. PHP writes the replacement session using filesystem operations such as pwrite() and ftruncate(). These operations are not guaranteed to behave as one atomic session commit. If the worker process terminates during or between these operations, stale bytes from the previous file may remain on disk. Researchers identified two useful interruption scenarios. In one, the worker dies while a larger replacement session is being written, leaving a prefix of the new state combined with the old file’s tail. In another, the new shorter state is written successfully but the worker terminates before ftruncate() removes the remaining old bytes. A later request that calls session_start() loads the resulting file as trusted server-side state. Carefully manipulated serialized lengths can then cause previously inert bytes in the old tail to be interpreted as additional session entries or serialized objects. The easiest externally reachable path identified by researchers involves PHP’s session upload-progress mechanism. When enabled, a multipart request containing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS can cause PHP to open and update session state during request parsing, before the application’s own PHP script begins. This means an application does not necessarily need to provide a dedicated upload function. The multipart request only needs to reach a PHP Web SAPI where upload progress is enabled, and the attacker must later reach an application path that loads the manipulated session. The attack still requires the session write to be interrupted at an advantageous point. Depthfirst demonstrated techniques involving memory pressure and worker termination to create the required partially updated session file. In one fresh test run, researchers produced the targeted object state after 11 attempts. This result describes their laboratory environment and should not be interpreted as a fixed exploitation success rate across real deployments. The CVE-2026-126714 PoC publicly demonstrates the core session-manipulation primitive using a harmless stdClass object. Security advisories now note that proof-of-concept material is publicly available, while Depthfirst has withheld key details of its separate PHP-native memory-corruption chain used to turn deserialization into end-to-end code execution. This distinction matters because arbitrary deserialization is not automatically equivalent to universal RCE. In a typical deployment, exploitation requires the target application to expose a suitable gadget chain that performs dangerous actions when attacker-controlled objects are reconstructed. Depthfirst states that its own RCE demonstration does not depend on an application-defined gadget. Instead, researchers identified a second flaw in PHP-native classes that provides memory corruption and eventually redirects execution inside the PHP worker. The underlying decoder and final heap-layout details remain withheld for coordinated disclosure. The issue is closely related to October’s PHP2Shell research. PHP released fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 on October 21, but those updates did not correct phpAfterShell. The earlier remediation restricted class resolution during the upload-progress callback, preventing the original exploitation technique from activating objects at that moment. However, PHP still wrote updated session data back to the same file, leaving the underlying interrupted-write behavior intact. Therefore, environments updated to PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, or 8.5.12 for PHP2Shell remain exposed and must apply the November security releases. For CVE-2026-126714 detection, defenders should monitor both the initial web behavior and subsequent host activity. Potential indicators include unusual multipart requests carrying session upload-progress fields, repeated manipulation of the same session identifier, abnormal PHP session parsing failures, worker terminations, out-of-memory events, and unexpected session corruption. Endpoint telemetry is particularly valuable for identifying successful exploitation. Security teams should investigate PHP-FPM, Apache, Nginx/PHP-FPM, or other PHP worker processes unexpectedly launching utilities such as sh, bash, cmd.exe, PowerShell, curl, wget, Python. Unexpected outbound network connections from PHP workers, newly created executable files, modifications to web application directories, persistence mechanisms, or credential-access behavior should significantly increase confidence that exploitation progressed beyond session corruption. Traditional CVE-2026-126714 IOCs such as fixed IP addresses, domains, malware hashes, or command-and-control infrastructure are currently of limited value. phpAfterShell is a vulnerability primitive rather than a malware campaign, and neither PHP nor Depthfirst has reported active exploitation in the wild. Organizations should therefore prioritize version and configuration exposure assessment alongside behavior-based detection rather than waiting for campaign-specific blocklists. Security teams looking for additional details for CVE-2026-126714 should verify the PHP runtime that actually handles production web requests. Container images, hosting platforms, application appliances, and custom runtime bundles may use a different PHP build from the command-line version available on the host. CVE-2026-126714 Mitigation The primary remediation is to install the PHP security release for the affected branch. PHP published the fixes on November 19, 2026. PHP branch Vulnerable versions Fixed version PHP 8.2 Before 8.2.36 8.2.36 PHP 8.3 Before 8.3.37 8.3.37 PHP 8.4 Before 8.4.28 8.4.28 PHP 8.5 Before 8.5.13 8.5.13 PHP 8.6 Pre-release builds affected during development 8.6.0 includes fix PHP’s official changelog identifies CVE-2026-126714 as a session vulnerability in which partially overwritten session files can lead to remote code execution. Organizations running containers should rebuild affected images and redeploy rather than merely updating packages on the underlying host. Administrators should then verify the PHP version used by production web workers because command-line PHP and the runtime serving HTTP requests can differ. The PHP development team has released security updates addressing CVE-2026-126714, a critical vulnerability dubbed phpAfterShell that can turn partially overwritten session files into an arbitrary deserialization primitive and potentially remote code execution. The flaw carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, Critical and affects PHP applications using the default file-based session handler.

Unlike a vulnerability confined to one CMS or framework, phpAfterShell exists in PHP itself. Applications built with WordPress, Laravel, custom PHP frameworks, or other software can therefore fall within the exposure scope if they run a vulnerable PHP release and store sessions as files. Applications using Redis, databases, or other non-file session handlers are outside this specific defect.

The vulnerability stems from how PHP updates existing session files. If an update is interrupted at the right moment, part of the new session data can overwrite the beginning of the file while bytes from the previous session remain at the end. PHP may later interpret this hybrid file as valid session state and deserialize attacker-controlled objects when the application calls session_start().

Successful exploitation requires several conditions, including attacker influence over session data, an interruption at a useful point during the write, and a suitable deserialization path. Depthfirst demonstrated that the primitive could be chained with a separate PHP-native memory-corruption technique to achieve code execution inside the PHP worker process.

Contact Sales

The issue is especially relevant because PHP’s session upload-progress feature can modify a session while PHP is still parsing an unauthenticated multipart request, before application code begins executing. This can give an attacker a pre-authentication path to manipulate file-backed session state under vulnerable configurations.

Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize vulnerability intelligence and accelerate hunting for exploitation behavior across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Detect CVE-2026-126714 by correlating suspicious multipart uploads, abnormal PHP session behavior, repeated worker crashes, and unexpected operating-system activity originating from PHP-FPM, Apache, or other PHP worker processes.

CVE-2026-126714 analysis

CVE-2026-126714 affects supported PHP branches prior to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13 when applications use file-backed sessions. PHP 8.6.0 was released with the correction included. Older PHP 8.1 and earlier releases are end-of-life and should be migrated to a supported branch rather than relied upon for ongoing security updates.

The vulnerability is located in PHP’s default files session save handler:

session.save_handler = files

PHP stores each session in a file such as:

/sess_

When session data changes, PHP serializes the new state and writes it into the existing file. The vulnerable design did not treat this update as a fully atomic transaction.

Under the default PHP session serialization format, multiple values are stored consecutively as records consisting of a session key and serialized value. Serialized strings contain explicit length information that tells PHP where a value ends and where parsing should continue.

That creates an important exploitation opportunity. Data that is harmless while positioned inside a serialized string can become active syntax when the beginning of the file is replaced with another carefully constructed session prefix.

Depthfirst researchers showed that two individually legitimate sessions could therefore be combined into a third valid but attacker-influenced session if the update process stops at the appropriate moment.

PHP writes the replacement session using filesystem operations such as pwrite() and ftruncate(). These operations are not guaranteed to behave as one atomic session commit. If the worker process terminates during or between these operations, stale bytes from the previous file may remain on disk.

Researchers identified two useful interruption scenarios. In one, the worker dies while a larger replacement session is being written, leaving a prefix of the new state combined with the old file’s tail. In another, the new shorter state is written successfully but the worker terminates before ftruncate() removes the remaining old bytes.

A later request that calls session_start() loads the resulting file as trusted server-side state. Carefully manipulated serialized lengths can then cause previously inert bytes in the old tail to be interpreted as additional session entries or serialized objects.

The easiest externally reachable path identified by researchers involves PHP’s session upload-progress mechanism. When enabled, a multipart request containing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS can cause PHP to open and update session state during request parsing, before the application’s own PHP script begins.

This means an application does not necessarily need to provide a dedicated upload function. The multipart request only needs to reach a PHP Web SAPI where upload progress is enabled, and the attacker must later reach an application path that loads the manipulated session.

The attack still requires the session write to be interrupted at an advantageous point. Depthfirst demonstrated techniques involving memory pressure and worker termination to create the required partially updated session file. In one fresh test run, researchers produced the targeted object state after 11 attempts. This result describes their laboratory environment and should not be interpreted as a fixed exploitation success rate across real deployments.

The CVE-2026-126714 PoC publicly demonstrates the core session-manipulation primitive using a harmless stdClass object. Security advisories now note that proof-of-concept material is publicly available, while Depthfirst has withheld key details of its separate PHP-native memory-corruption chain used to turn deserialization into end-to-end code execution.

This distinction matters because arbitrary deserialization is not automatically equivalent to universal RCE. In a typical deployment, exploitation requires the target application to expose a suitable gadget chain that performs dangerous actions when attacker-controlled objects are reconstructed.

Depthfirst states that its own RCE demonstration does not depend on an application-defined gadget. Instead, researchers identified a second flaw in PHP-native classes that provides memory corruption and eventually redirects execution inside the PHP worker. The underlying decoder and final heap-layout details remain withheld for coordinated disclosure.

The issue is closely related to October’s PHP2Shell research. PHP released fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 on October 21, but those updates did not correct phpAfterShell.

The earlier remediation restricted class resolution during the upload-progress callback, preventing the original exploitation technique from activating objects at that moment. However, PHP still wrote updated session data back to the same file, leaving the underlying interrupted-write behavior intact.

Potential indicators include unusual multipart requests carrying session upload-progress fields, repeated manipulation of the same session identifier, abnormal PHP session parsing failures, worker terminations, out-of-memory events, and unexpected session corruption.

Endpoint telemetry is particularly valuable for identifying successful exploitation. Security teams should investigate PHP-FPM, Apache, Nginx/PHP-FPM, or other PHP worker processes unexpectedly launching utilities such as sh, bash, cmd.exe, PowerShell, curl, wget, Python.

Unexpected outbound network connections from PHP workers, newly created executable files, modifications to web application directories, persistence mechanisms, or credential-access behavior should significantly increase confidence that exploitation progressed beyond session corruption.

Traditional CVE-2026-126714 IOCs such as fixed IP addresses, domains, malware hashes, or command-and-control infrastructure are currently of limited value. phpAfterShell is a vulnerability primitive rather than a malware campaign, and neither PHP nor Depthfirst has reported active exploitation in the wild.

Organizations should therefore prioritize version and configuration exposure assessment alongside behavior-based detection rather than waiting for campaign-specific blocklists.

Container images, hosting platforms, application appliances, and custom runtime bundles may use a different PHP build from the command-line version available on the host.

items.title: CVE-2026-132825: Ruby2Shell Heap Overflow Can Lead to Remote Code Execution
items.summary: Ruby maintainers have released security updates addressing CVE-2026-132825, a memory-corruption vulnerability dubbed Ruby2Shell that affects string case conversion in the Ruby interpreter. The issue is a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow that can be triggered when Ruby changes the case of specially crafted strings in certain legacy single-byte encodings, including ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252. The Ruby project rates the underlying GitHub Security Advisory as Critical and states that proofs of concept have demonstrated remote code execution in some scenarios. The published CVE record currently carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 7.4, High , reflecting a narrower exploitability assessment. This distinction matters: the memory corruption is confirmed, but practical remote exploitation depends on how an application accepts and processes attacker-controlled strings. The flaw was patched alongside six additional vulnerabilities in Ruby’s regular expression engine and string-conversion logic. Fixed releases are Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 . Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive upstream fixes. Contact Sales Ruby is embedded throughout modern web and developer infrastructure. Rails applications, classic-style Sinatra deployments, and self-hosted products that bundle Ruby can therefore inherit the flaw even when their own application code has not changed. Veria Labs says it independently demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against stock Rails. Organizations can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize emerging vulnerability intelligence and accelerate threat hunting across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Detect CVE-2026-132825 by correlating suspicious legacy-encoded HTTP input with Ruby process crashes, memory-corruption events, and unexpected child-process or network activity originating from web application workers. CVE-2026-132825 analysis CVE-2026-132825 affects Ruby releases before 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10. The vulnerable code has existed since Ruby 2.4.0, meaning unsupported Ruby branches can also contain the bug even though they are no longer receiving upstream security fixes. The root cause lies in Ruby’s case-conversion implementation for several legacy single-byte character encodings. In these encodings, the German sharp s character, ß, can expand from one byte of input into two output characters, SS, during uppercasing. The vulnerable conversion loop verifies that there is room for one byte in the destination buffer, writes the first S, and later writes the second S without performing another bounds check. Ruby allocates the output buffer with limited additional space, so carefully sized input containing enough expansion characters can cause the final byte to be written just beyond the allocated heap region. Veria Labs reports that an input containing 21 sharp-s characters can cross the buffer boundary and create the one-byte overwrite. The affected path is reachable through methods including upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold), and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings follow a different code path and are not affected by this specific vulnerability. The size of the primitive is small but still security-relevant. A one-byte heap overwrite can corrupt adjacent heap metadata or nearby objects, and the converted result can also lead to an out-of-bounds read. Whether this becomes RCE depends heavily on the memory allocator, process layout, target application, Ruby version, surrounding heap objects, and the attacker’s ability to repeatedly shape memory. Veria Labs likewise states that Rails and classic-style Sinatra are exposed by default on affected Ruby releases, while plain Rack and other frameworks are not necessarily exposed unless application code performs the relevant case conversion on attacker-controlled data. A vulnerable Ruby runtime therefore does not automatically prove that every application running on it is remotely exploitable. The CVE-2026-132825 PoC situation is also evolving. Ruby maintainers confirm that they are aware of proofs of concept capable of achieving RCE in some scenarios, but the main remote exploit developed by Veria Labs has not yet been released publicly. Veria currently states that it plans to publish an RCE demonstration against stock Rails on November 25, 2026, or later if major vendors have not yet shipped fixes. Independent public research has reproduced the memory-corruption primitive and heap effects locally but explicitly notes that it has not verified the same remote delivery path. Defenders should therefore treat remote exploitability as credible without assuming that a reliable universal web exploit is already publicly available. For CVE-2026-132825 detection, security teams should combine web telemetry with runtime and endpoint evidence. Potential indicators include requests carrying unusual ISO-8859 or Windows-125x encodings, repeated application crashes following crafted parameters or multipart requests, allocator faults, segmentation failures, and abnormal Ruby worker restarts. Successful exploitation would produce stronger endpoint signals. Ruby, Puma, Passenger, Unicorn, Sidekiq, or other Ruby application processes unexpectedly spawning sh, bash, curl, wget, Python, or other utilities should be investigated immediately. Unexpected outbound network connections, file drops, persistence changes, or credential-access activity originating from Ruby web workers can indicate that memory corruption progressed to code execution. Traditional CVE-2026-132825 IOCs are currently limited because Ruby2Shell is a vulnerability rather than a campaign tied to fixed attacker infrastructure. There are no authoritative attacker IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or command-and-control indicators associated with confirmed exploitation. Exposure analysis and behavior-based monitoring are therefore more useful than static blocklists. Several widely deployed self-hosted products bundle Ruby internally. As of November 20, Veria Labs lists fixed releases for GitLab, Mastodon, OpenProject, and the Discourse base image, while GitHub Enterprise Server and Chatwoot were still shown without fixed releases on its tracking page. Organizations should follow each product vendor’s advisory instead of manually replacing an embedded Ruby runtime unless that approach is explicitly supported. Security teams looking for additional details for CVE-2026-132825 should verify the exact Ruby runtime used by the running application, not merely the system-wide interpreter. Containers, appliances, background workers, CI/CD systems, and vendor products can ship separate Ruby installations that remain vulnerable after the host package has been updated. CVE-2026-132825 Mitigation The primary remediation is to upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10 or later. The Ruby project states that no equivalent security update will be released for Ruby 3.2 and older branches because they have reached end of life. For CVE-2026-132825 mitigation, organizations should inventory every Ruby runtime used by production applications, rebuild container images, update pinned versions in Dockerfiles and .ruby-version files, restart application processes, and verify that the running process is actually using the patched interpreter. Ruby branch Vulnerable versions Fixed release 4.0 4.0.0–4.0.9 4.0.10 3.4 3.4.0–3.4.12 3.4.13 3.3 3.3.13 and earlier 3.3.14 3.2 and older End-of-life, including releases back to 2.4.0 Upgrade to a supported branch Organizations operating self-hosted software that bundles Ruby should install the vendor-provided application update rather than assuming an operating-system Ruby package upgrade fixes the embedded runtime. Where no vendor fix is available, temporarily reducing public exposure through a VPN, reverse-proxy allowlist, or equivalent access control can lower risk until an update is released. Ruby’s official advisory does not provide a complete workaround. Avoiding attacker-controlled input in vulnerable legacy encodings may reduce exposure, but this is application-dependent and should not replace patching. WAF or request-normalization controls can provide additional friction but should be treated as compensating controls rather than a guaranteed fix. Because UTF-8 does not use the vulnerable code path, applications that strictly normalize external strings to UTF-8 before affected case-conversion operations may have lower exposure. However, defenders should validate actual application behavior rather than infer safety from a nominal UTF-8 default, particularly where middleware or request parsers can preserve attacker-supplied encoding information. After remediation, review logs for unexplained Ruby worker crashes or suspicious process execution during the period when the application was exposed. If a Ruby process spawned system commands or created unexpected outbound connections, treat the server as potentially compromised rather than assuming the runtime update alone resolves the incident. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. FAQ What is CVE-2026-132825 and how does it work? CVE-2026-132825, commonly called Ruby2Shell, is a one-byte heap buffer overflow in Ruby’s string case-conversion code for certain legacy single-byte encodings. When a character such as ß expands into two bytes during case conversion, the vulnerable loop can write the second byte beyond the allocated output buffer. Under suitable heap conditions, that memory corruption may potentially be developed into arbitrary code execution. When was CVE-2026-132825 first discovered? The exact private discovery date has not been publicly disclosed. Ruby credits Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics and Anthropic with reporting the underlying flaw, while Veria Labs says it discovered the issue independently and was the first to demonstrate RCE. Ruby released the fixed versions on November 18, 2026, and the CVE record was published on November 19. What is the impact of CVE-2026-132825 on systems? The immediate impact is heap memory corruption and potential process crashes. Under favorable conditions, the one-byte overwrite can be used to corrupt adjacent memory and potentially execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the Ruby application process. Ruby maintainers confirm that PoCs have achieved RCE in some scenarios, but exploitability varies substantially by application and runtime environment. Can CVE-2026-132825 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Systems remain exposed when they run Ruby versions older than 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10 and expose an application path that performs vulnerable case conversion on attacker-controlled strings in affected encodings. End-of-life Ruby versions can also contain the flaw and will not receive upstream fixes. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-132825? Upgrade to Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, or 4.0.10 or later, rebuild containers, restart Ruby application processes, and verify the actual runtime version used in production. For products that bundle Ruby, install the vendor’s fixed application release. If no update is available yet, reduce public exposure and restrict access until the vendor provides a supported fix.
