Lisa Hanawalt's "I Can't Stop Thinking About Horses and Sex" ( permalink ) The title of animator Lisa Hanawalt's new graphic memoir I Can't Stop Thinking About Horses and Sex is a perfect encapsulation of the book's contents: a frank, self-aware, funny, horny, horsey exploration of Hanawalt's life, relationships, gender, and digestive issues: https://drawnandquarterly.com/books/i-cant-stop-thinking-about-horses-and-sex/ Hanawalt is probably best known as the character designer for Bojack Horseman , but is also much loved in animation circles for her all-too-short-lived show Tuca & Bertie : https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuca_%26_Bertie She lived with the comedian/podcaster/showrunner Adam "Ruins Everything" Conover for 14 years, and the memoir revolves around the couple's breakup. As the title promises, Hanawalt is also a lifelong horse-lover, who spent her childhood developing scars on her knees and calluses on the tops of her feet from endless all-fours sessions of pretending to be a horse. As an adult, she rides at the Los Angeles Equestrian Center, where she meets other horse people, who are beautifully depicted as the mix of posh sociopaths, obsessive animal-lovers, and lovable misfits (my daughter's middle school was around the corner from the LAEC and she grew up shoveling manure and tacking up at a teaching barn there; I can vouch for Hanawalt's faithful portrayal of the vibe). Horses are Hanawalt's touchstone, the thing that brings her thoughts and emotions back into equilibrium, no matter what life throws at her. Eventually – inevitably – she acquires a horse, and just as inevitably, that horse proves to be her savior and her heartbreak. Horses are massive, majestic, impossibly powerful animals that are nevertheless forever on the verge of death, one weird disease or inexplicable fall from being maimed for life or keeling over. The story of Hanawalt's pony Juni is intertwined with the story of her and Conover's breakup and her post-breakup relationships. Both threads of the tale are developed through beautiful, extremely funny, deeply personal vignettes that are brought to life by Hanawalt's art, which depicts bodies (animal, human, and animalistic human avatars) as hilarious, weird, and sexy all at once. These two motifs criss-cross as we journey through Hanawalt's dating life, her childhood sexual trauma, her IBS, and her fears and hopes about her fertility (two of the major subplots involve Hanawalt's experiences with egg-freezing and bowel problems, and the way that the medical system treats women). Hanawalt has a gift for compact, revealing character studies that leave the reader feeling both warm affection and exasperation with everyone in her life (including Hanawalt herself). It's a world without heroes and villains, where flaws and virtues are almost always flip-sides of the same coin. Everyone is crazy sometimes, including Hanawalt, and Hanawalt is self-aware enough to know when she's getting in her own way, and even why that happens, and also (just like all of us) can't always stop herself from tripping herself up. Hanawalt's written and drawn a wise, funny, horny book that wrings comedy and insight out of trauma and melancholy. It's a gorgeous read that lingers. Hanawalt isn't the only person who made smart, funny media out of her and Conover's breakup. Conover's comedy special about the breakup and its aftermath is called "Big Divorce Energy" and it was released the same week that Can't Stop Thinking hit the shelves: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CVB-SUX7zgk I saw Conover perform this set live and it was terrific – and it got even better by the time he recorded it for the special. It makes for a perfect bookend for Hanawalt's memoir, a fact that both Conover and Hanawalt affirm in a lovely, warm conversation they recorded for Conover's Factually podcast. It's an interview that raises the bar for the kind of affection and even love a mature couple can salvage from a breakup: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BUXEDUiICM4 The book itself is from Montreal's Drawn and Quarterly, who have a well-deserved reputation for publishing quality graphic novels, especially memoirs. D&Q always puts together a beautiful physical artifact, and Can't Stop Thinking is no exception: a handsome hardcover with luxurious, thick semi-matte pages and a bookmark ribbon sewn into the binding. It's the perfect gift for any friend going through a breakup (or thinking about buying a horse). items.title: Signal Restricts Screenshots to protect User Privacy from AI assistants
items.summary: Signal is restricting screenshots on iOS 27 and some Android devices to stop built-in AI assistants from reading private chats through screen capture. The encrypted messaging app is targeting Apple’s Siri AI and assistants such as Google Gemini. On Android, the block turns on when Signal detects an assistant trying to read the screen. The change addresses what happens after a message arrives. End-to-end encryption protects messages as they travel between devices, but Signal must show readable text when someone opens a chat. An assistant that can read the screen does not have to break that encryption to see the message. It can capture the same text the recipient sees. On iOS 27, Signal’s “Block Siri AI” setting prevents Siri from scanning Signal content and blocks screenshots inside the app and in the App Switcher. On Android, Signal automatically turns on “Screen security” when it detects an assistant seeking screen access. Signal says detection varies across Android versions, so the protection does not work the same way on every phone. The move follows Signal’s 2025 decision to block screenshots by default in its Windows 11 desktop app to keep chats out of Microsoft Recall’s searchable history. Other developers took a different route. As Cyber Security News reported, Brave blocked Microsoft Recall while preserving regular screenshots . Signal Restricts Screenshots Apple says Siri’s onscreen awareness lets it answer questions or act on what users are viewing. Google’s Gemini help page says some screen actions upload visible content to give the assistant context. That does not mean either assistant routinely records every Signal chat. The risk is that once an assistant captures a message, Signal cannot control how that copy is handled. Users can turn off the protection in Signal’s privacy settings to take screenshots again, but doing so can also expose messages from other people in the chat. The Electronic Frontier Foundation points to a separate option on iOS 27.2: open Settings → Siri → Excluded Apps and add Signal to block Siri’s access, including on-screen awareness. Screenshot blocking does not cover every route to private data. Signal says it cannot offer the same protection on macOS and warns that an assistant may still reach content already saved on a device. In related coverage, Meta’s Muse read Signal message text through Android notifications and Mac permissions without breaking Signal’s encryption. Signal is asking Apple, Google and Microsoft to give developers a clear way to opt out of AI access to screens, files and notifications without disabling ordinary features such as screenshots. It also wants better documentation about what assistants can read and where that data goes. The distinction matters for anyone sharing sensitive information. A screenshot block can close one route into a private chat, but it cannot decide what a phone shows in a notification or what permissions another app receives. Those controls sit with the operating system, which is why Signal is pressing platform makers for stronger limits. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. items.title: Frida 17.27.4 Released
items.summary: A compiler release: a much more complete fs module for agents, thanks to @std-microblock and @ChiChou , two fixes for patterns compiled into agents, and a hang on entrypoints with a colon in their name. frida-fs Frida.Compiler bundles frida-fs , our implementation of Node.js’ fs module for GumJS, and this release moves it from 7.1.1 to 8.1.2. That brings: mkdir() , rename() , copyFile() , appendFile() , chmod() , chown() , utimes() , realpath() , symlink() , truncate() , access() and existsSync() , contributed by @std-microblock . The start , end and highWaterMark options of createReadStream() , contributed by @ChiChou . A fix for read streams without an end yielding no data on Windows, where QuickJS evaluates Infinity to NaN . A fix for readlink() on procfs links such as /proc/self , which failed with “invalid size”. The buffer was sized from what lstat() reports, and procfs reports zero for its links. Field reads also got cheaper, by passing offsets to pointer reads rather than allocating a NativePointer per field. That means an agent using fs built with this compiler needs Frida 17.20 or newer at runtime. Thanks, both! Patterns A pattern can describe both the on-disk and the in-memory form of a format, and pick between them by whether MEMORY is defined. A pattern compiled into an agent decodes live memory, so it is now defined there, as pattern queries already assumed. Addresses past 2^53, such as a kernel’s, went through parseInt() on their way into the compiled pattern and lost their low bits, so std::mem::base_address() and addressof() were off by up to 2 KiB there. They are now parsed as a BigInt , and only narrowed when that is lossless. Entrypoints with a colon Compiling an entrypoint whose name holds a colon hung. esbuild renames such an output, so our bundler couldn’t find it and panicked inside esbuild’s end-of-build callback, where the panic deadlocked on the very build it was ending. We now tell esbuild what to name the output, and report a failure there as an error. Enjoy! Changelog compiler: Bump frida-fs to 8.1.2. Thanks @std-microblock and @ChiChou ! compiler: Define MEMORY for patterns in agents. compiler: Keep wide pattern offsets exact. compiler: Name the entrypoint’s output explicitly, fixing a hang on entrypoints with a colon in their name.
items.summary_html:
A compiler release: a much more complete fs module for agents, thanks to @std-microblock and @ChiChou, two fixes for patterns compiled into agents, and a hang on entrypoints with a colon in their name.

frida-fs

Frida.Compiler bundles frida-fs, our implementation of Node.js’ fs module for GumJS, and this release moves it from 7.1.1 to 8.1.2. That brings:

  • mkdir(), rename(), copyFile(), appendFile(), chmod(), chown(), utimes(), realpath(), symlink(), truncate(), access() and existsSync(), contributed by @std-microblock.
  • The start, end and highWaterMark options of createReadStream(), contributed by @ChiChou.
  • A fix for read streams without an end yielding no data on Windows, where QuickJS evaluates Infinity to NaN.
  • A fix for readlink() on procfs links such as /proc/self, which failed with “invalid size”. The buffer was sized from what lstat() reports, and procfs reports zero for its links.

Field reads also got cheaper, by passing offsets to pointer reads rather than allocating a NativePointer per field. That means an agent using fs built with this compiler needs Frida 17.20 or newer at runtime.

Thanks, both!

Patterns

A pattern can describe both the on-disk and the in-memory form of a format, and pick between them by whether MEMORY is defined. A pattern compiled into an agent decodes live memory, so it is now defined there, as pattern queries already assumed.

Addresses past 2^53, such as a kernel’s, went through parseInt() on their way into the compiled pattern and lost their low bits, so std::mem::base_address() and addressof() were off by up to 2 KiB there. They are now parsed as a BigInt, and only narrowed when that is lossless.

Entrypoints with a colon

Compiling an entrypoint whose name holds a colon hung. esbuild renames such an output, so our bundler couldn’t find it and panicked inside esbuild’s end-of-build callback, where the panic deadlocked on the very build it was ending. We now tell esbuild what to name the output, and report a failure there as an error.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • compiler: Bump frida-fs to 8.1.2. Thanks @std-microblock and @ChiChou!
  • compiler: Define MEMORY for patterns in agents.
  • compiler: Keep wide pattern offsets exact.
  • compiler: Name the entrypoint’s output explicitly, fixing a hang on entrypoints with a colon in their name.

items.title: Palo Alto Confirms Java Vulnerability Impacts Privilege Threat Analytics and Remote Access Connector
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that a critical Java vulnerability affects Idira Privilege Threat Analytics, Remote Access Connector, and on-premises HTML5 Gateway products. Tracked as CVE-2026-114938 , the flaw could let a remote attacker run code without signing in when specific hardware and software conditions are met. The company’s security advisory, published November 20, assigns the issue a CVSS score of 9.2 and moderate response urgency. Palo Alto Networks says it is not aware of malicious exploitation and continues to review its wider product range and cloud services. The flaw sits in the optimized Base64 decoder inside HotSpot, the Java Virtual Machine used by affected Oracle Java SE , Oracle GraalVM, and OpenJDK releases. Base64 converts binary data into text for storage or transfer. Specially crafted input can make the decoder write beyond its assigned heap memory, creating a possible path to remote code execution. This memory error falls under CWE-787, an out-of-bounds write . In simple terms, the decoder can overwrite memory outside the space reserved for its output. Such writes can damage data, crash software, or allow unwanted code to run. Palo Alto Confirms Critical Java Flaw Successful exploitation requires an affected Java release running on an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. The accelerated Base64 decoder must be enabled, and the application must pass untrusted input to it. Palo Alto says no special product configuration is required, but these underlying conditions still apply. Cyber Security News previously covered the issue in its Java4Shell vulnerability report , explaining why the affected Java runtime and processor features matter when assessing exposure. Privilege Threat Analytics 15.2 releases before 15.2.3 are affected. Customers should install version 15.2.3 or later. Those running the 14.6 branch should upgrade to 14.6.4 or move to 15.2.3 or later. All releases in the 15.0 branch are affected, and customers should upgrade to 15.2.3 or later. Remote Access Connector versions before 1.1.1002202 require an update to that release or later. The separate Remote Access Connector CLI needs version 1.1.3701 or later. Palo Alto released fixes for affected 15.2.2 and 15.0.3 installations, with no known workaround, while managing updates for ADEM Infrastructure, Prisma Access-MSP, Prisma AIRS, Idira EPM SaaS, Idira Remote Access, and hosted HTML5 Gateway, requiring no customer action. PAN-OS-based firewalls, Panorama, WF-500-B, and PAN-DB private cloud appliances are not affected. This separates the Java issue from earlier Palo Alto PAN-OS code execution vulnerabilities . Customers remain responsible for updating custom Java applications, third-party tools, and integration components in their environments. Fixing a listed Palo Alto product does not remove that separate responsibility. The vendor directs customers to follow each software provider’s security guidance while its broader product review continues. items.title: ClamAV Patches 10 High-Severity Vulnerabilities That Could Let Attackers Crash Antivirus Scanners
items.summary: ClamAV has released versions 1.5.5 and 1.4.7 to fix 10 security flaws that could let attackers crash antivirus scanners , trap scan workers in endless loops, or drain system resources using crafted files. Published on November 18, 2026, the updates also address memory errors that could expose process data or corrupt memory during scanning. The fixes cover email handling, document parsing, archive extraction, and executable unpacking. Both releases patch all 10 CVEs. However, the official ClamAV release notice does not provide CVSS scores or label every flaw as high severity. It also does not report active exploitation, so the documented risks should not be confused with confirmed attacks. CVE-2026-76422 affects the bridge between Rust and C logging code. Attacker-controlled text could be treated as a C format string rather than plain data, causing a crash, memory disclosure, or memory corruption. The flaw dates back to version 0.105.0. CVE-2026-76411 affects URL processing when ClamAV scans crafted emails with full-hash phishing database entries loaded. Incorrect length tracking could write beyond a stack buffer. This condition matters because the vulnerable path depends on those database entries being present. Three other flaws affect packed files and compressed content. CVE-2026-76415 could make the yC unpacker read beyond a heap buffer after an offset calculation underflows. ClamAV Fixes 10 High-Severity Flaws CVE-2026-76421 could cause an out-of-bounds heap write while handling LZX data in CHM archives. CVE-2026-76430 could trigger similar writes during UPX decompression and Windows executable rebuilding. These fixes follow earlier ClamAV parser vulnerabilities that disrupted antivirus scanning . The recurring concern is that security software must inspect untrusted files, making errors in its file readers a direct threat to scanning availability. Several patched bugs can stop useful scanning without relying on a memory overwrite. CVE-2026-76414 allows cyclic directory data inside a CHM file to trigger an endless scan loop. CVE-2026-76416 affects InstallShield archives, where invalid file counts and offsets could keep a scan worker occupied. Two issues affect OLE2 documents. CVE-2026-76417 could exhaust the process stack through deeply nested document properties. CVE-2026-76515 could cause excessive CPU use while following directory chains. The stack exhaustion flaw reaches back to ClamAV 0.71, showing how long some affected code has remained in use. CVE ID Affected Component Vulnerability / Impact Affected Versions CVE-2026-76422 Rust-to-C logging Format string flaw could expose memory or corrupt data. 0.105.0–1.5.4 CVE-2026-76411 URL canonicalization Stack buffer overflow during email scanning. 0.94–1.5.4 CVE-2026-76415 yC executable unpacker Out-of-bounds heap read. 0.96–1.5.4 CVE-2026-76414 CHM directory parsing Infinite scan loops causing denial of service. 0.100.0–1.5.4 CVE-2026-76416 InstallShield archive parsing Malformed archives could disrupt scan workers. 0.96–1.5.4 CVE-2026-76417 OLE2 property parsing Deeply nested properties could crash the scanner. 0.71–1.5.4 CVE-2026-76421 LZX decompression (CHM) Out-of-bounds heap write. 0.80–1.5.4 CVE-2026-76430 UPX decompression and PE rebuilding Out-of-bounds heap writes. 0.94.1–1.5.4 CVE-2026-76516 XAR archive extraction Could exhaust temporary storage. 0.98–1.5.4 CVE-2026-76515 OLE2 directory-chain parsing Excessive CPU usage could disrupt scanning. 0.98.1–1.5.4 Separately, CVE-2026-76516 could let crafted XAR archives exhaust temporary storage because extraction writes occurred before file-count and scan-size limits were enforced. The patch moves those checks ahead of writes. Cyber Security News previously covered an OLE2 parsing flaw that could crash ClamAV . The latest OLE2 bugs are separate issues involving stack depth and directory traversal, not that earlier decryption error. Administrators should install ClamAV 1.5.5 or the 1.4.7 long-term support release from the official downloads page. Updating malware signatures alone does not replace the engine fixes. ClamAV states that both the engine and virus database must stay current. The releases also restore ClamAV submissions, improve OpenSSL 4 support, and update Rust dependencies. Alpine and Debian container images are offered through Docker Hub. However, ClamAV warns that updated images may appear later than release files. items.title: Hackers Exploit Misconfigured Temenos Banking Platform to Deploy Web Shells Without Passwords
items.summary: Hackers gained administrator access to an internet-facing Temenos Quantum Fabric deployment without a password and used the banking platform’s own tools to install malicious Java components. The campaign, dubbed BankWeaver, turned a service that should have been private into a route to the application server and its connected systems. Investigators confirmed one compromise at a financial services institution. Six other banks across Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and the Americas appeared to have the same configuration and internet exposure. Investigators did not confirm that any of those six banks were compromised. The suspected exposure matters because Quantum Fabric, formerly Kony Fabric, links customer-facing web and mobile apps to identity systems, payment services, databases, and customer records. Researchers from Forescout’s Vedere Labs identified the malware while investigating the breach in early September. In its November 19 report, Forescout named the two components FabricShell and FabricShadow. One let the attackers run commands and query databases; the other gathered information about the server and sent it out of the network. Hackers Exploit Misconfigured Temenos Banking Platform Forescout traced the intrusion to a Fabric authentication service that issued privileged tokens but was configured to accept anonymous access. A token is a digital credential that tells a service what its holder is allowed to do. Here, a token meant for anonymous application access was accepted across an administrative trust boundary. The attackers gained administrator privileges without supplying valid login credentials. With those privileges, the attackers abused Fabric’s support for custom Java integrations. The platform loaded the malicious code as part of its normal service framework, giving it access to the application’s network and database connections. Earlier reporting on VMware vCenter web shells describes a separate campaign in which attackers also planted backdoors in enterprise infrastructure. FabricShell was registered as a Fabric service. It could run operating system commands, return their output, and submit database queries. Forescout found hardcoded PostgreSQL connection details tied to another victim, raising the possibility of both reading and modifying data. Attack flow (Source – Forescout) That capability is not proof that customer records were stolen. Separate reporting on Lazarus IIS web shells shows how similar tools can combine server control with database access. FabricShadow ran before the application processed data requests. It collected details such as the hostname, network interfaces, Java version, and service account, then saved a local copy and sent the findings to remote infrastructure. Forescout identified more than 30 IP addresses used during the campaign and said the operators routed activity through compromised devices and victim servers. Access configuration Temenos attributed the behavior to the access configuration, according to Forescout. The vendor released updates and guidance to make the service private and advised customers to restrict internet access to Spotlight and Fabric’s administrative and authentication services. Closing that route prevents the same exposure from being abused again, but it does not remove an implant already installed. Defenders should check for unexpected Java package registrations, service imports, and application publishing events. Java or Tomcat launching shells, downloaders, or network utilities is another signal worth investigating alongside outbound traffic and application logs. Earlier NSA web shell guidance likewise stresses checking both internal and internet-facing servers for persistent backdoors. Where investigators find signs of compromise, Forescout recommends preserving logs, memory, and suspicious packages before cleanup, revoking active sessions, rotating exposed credentials, and rebuilding affected nodes from known-good images. The key check before restoring service is whether anonymous access is confined to its intended public workflow and can no longer yield administrative privileges. items.title: Catching Ransomware: Introducing encrypts-files and Stricter MITRE ATT&CK T1486
items.summary: When we search for ransomware samples during an investigation or detection test, we usually want to answer a direct question: Did this file actually encrypt user documents when executed? Modern ransomware families implement file encryption in many different ways. While commodity builders may call standard operating system cryptographic APIs, contemporary Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) payloads written in Rust, Go, C++, or .NET frequently embed statically linked AES, ChaCha20-Poly1305, RSA, or custom intermittent encryption routines that never touch OS crypto libraries. At the same time, benign installers, browsers, and updaters legitimately use cryptography and write thousands of temporary files during normal execution. This week, we rolled out three updates across VirusTotal and Google Threat Intelligence to identify malware that encrypts user files: New encrypts-files Tag Across Windows and macOS Sandboxes: A cipher-agnostic behavioral trait ( behaviour_tags:encrypts_files ) and file-level search tag ( tag:encrypts-files ) emitted across CAPE Sandbox , Zenbox , and macOS Mirage only when dynamic analysis confirms real encryption of user documents. Stricter MITRE ATT&CK T1486 Gating in CAPE Sandbox: Previously, generic CAPE file-churn signatures mapped high-volume file deletes, overwrites, or moves directly to T1486 . Newly scanned CAPE reports now require verified user-file encryption before emitting those T1486 mappings, cutting CAPE-only daily T1486 hits from 1,039/day (78.5% with 0 AV detections) to 0 on benign files and reducing false positives across platform-wide T1486 volume by 97.6% (from 7,238 to 171 files per day). Real-Time VirusTotal Livehunt Support: Real-time YARA-X matching on sandbox reports via vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES . Figure 1: High-level overview of how CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage verify user-document encryption before emitting tag:encrypts-files and gating CAPE T1486 . How Cipher-Agnostic File-Encryption Verification Works Across CAPE Sandbox (Windows), Zenbox (Windows), and macOS Mirage (Apple Silicon), each sandbox environment contains realistic user documents across standard user profile directories. During and after detonation, our sandboxes apply three verification gates before emitting encrypts-files (and before CAPE emits generic T1486 mappings): Content Destruction and Entropy Verification (Cipher-Agnostic): Rather than hooking OS cryptographic APIs, each sandbox inspects modified user-file content on disk using format-aware verification tailored to its platform. Depending on the file type and sandbox, checks evaluate destroyed file structures, elevated entropy, or non-text byte patterns alongside corroborating ransomware behaviors without relying on a single fixed entropy threshold. Because verification evaluates the resulting files on disk, it catches AES, ChaCha20, intermittent encryption, and XOR ciphers alike. Coordinated Ransomware Extension Renames: Many ransomware families read original user documents, write encrypted copies under a uniform new extension (for example, .k404 , .lkd , .INC , .BLWZ , or .heartbreaker ), and delete the originals. Our sandboxes correlate reads, writes, moves, and unlinks across user directories to confirm coordinated encryption renames across user documents. Benign File-Churn Exclusion Guards: Self-extracting archives, software installers, compilers, browser caches, and logs are explicitly excluded when they only generate routine temporary or application files rather than encrypting user documents. Similarly, dropping a README.txt file or calling crypto APIs alone never triggers encrypts-files without corroborated document encryption. Real-World Ransomware Caught in Action Across 328,257 newly submitted unique files (405,469 total files including rescans) analyzed in CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage since November 17, tag:encrypts-files matched 55 files and surfaced in-the-wild and validation payloads across Windows executables, Python scripts, DLLs, compressed archives (ZIP and RAR), and a rescanned Apple Silicon macOS binary with zero benign software false positives across all 55 manually reviewed matches (alongside 0 benign false positives across 9,976 random CAPE reports and 400 macOS Mirage runs in pre-rollout backtesting). Below are three examples you can inspect on VirusTotal. 1. Catching Zero- and Low-Detection In-the-Wild Lockers: The .k404 Campaign and lkd.exe Static signatures often lag behind script-based or freshly compiled lockers. In an active .k404 extortion campaign submitted on November 17-18, Python locker fb0982bb9f5d5700685dcf4e99ff695f4593fbc3e3d0359d4c2baf23c545f354 ( system_update.pyw ) was flagged by 0 out of 75 static antivirus engines at the time of analysis, while companion PE binary 3dd45ab8e2f9c1af773a75221d792fb78870764419170e9c9c5941160364c700 (K404T_Fidye.exe) had 10 / 75 detections and separate Windows locker a8c2402ef3ae115300f5428712ccb0b5461f4a2f14b5bfdfbe08d5ad86bd3087 (lkd.exe) had 3 / 75 at the time of analysis. Figure 2: VirusTotal Behavior report for undetected Python locker system_update.pyw ( fb0982bb9f5d5700685dcf4e99ff695f4593fbc3e3d0359d4c2baf23c545f354 , 0 / 59 AV on GUI at capture), showing encrypts-files, T1486, and Desktop user files encrypted with the .k404 extension. When detonated in Zenbox, system_update.pyw runs under pythonw.exe from AppData\Roaming\WindowsSystemUpdate\, self-deletes, and rewrites Desktop user files into .k404 ciphertext, while K404T_Fidye.exe and lkd.exe encrypt user documents in CAPE Sandbox using .k404 and .lkd extensions alongside k404t.txt and read_me_restore.txt ransom notes. In CAPE Sandbox, verified encryption sets both tag:encrypts-files and T1486 . Note that Zenbox, macOS Mirage, and third-party sandboxes (such as Dr.Web vxCube or VMRay) keep their own rule-level T1486 mappings, so a file can carry T1486 from another sandbox rule without tag:encrypts-files. 2. Enterprise RaaS & High-Speed Windows Encryptors: INC Ransom and BlackWizardLock Modern Windows ransomware families optimize encryption speed using asynchronous I/O and multi-threaded directory queues. In sample d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645 ( INC Ransom ), CAPE Sandbox captures the payload binding user files to Windows I/O Completion Ports (IOCP), rewriting user documents into .INC files, and dropping INC-README.txt across directories. Figure 3: INC Ransom ( d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645 ) Behavior report showing T1486 user-file encryption and user documents rewritten with the .INC extension. Similarly, sample 98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e ( BlackWizardLock ) executes unpacked payload code from dynamically allocated memory, stages temporary .~BLWZ.tmp files, overwrites user documents with .BLWZ extensions (such as bitaddress.pdf.BLWZ and cover-letter-uidev.docx.BLWZ ), and presents a full-screen Russian extortion lock screen that directs victims to @seedware on Telegram and threatens to destroy the Master Boot Record (MBR) after five wrong key attempts. Figure 4: BlackWizardLock ( 98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e ) Behavior report showing encrypts-files, T1486 impact, and user documents encrypted into .BLWZ files. 3. Native Apple Silicon macOS Ransomware: Heartbreaker (Historical macOS Sample Rescanned in macOS Mirage, 16 / 75 AV at Analysis) While native macOS ransomware is rare in the wild compared to Windows, re-analyzing historical macOS samples validates Apple Silicon coverage. Sample 6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18 (first submitted in May 2025 and rescanned in macOS Mirage) is a self-signed 64-bit ARM64 Mach-O binary detected by 16 out of 75 antivirus engines at the time of analysis . Figure 5: Native macOS Heartbreaker ransomware ( 6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18 ) Behavior report in macOS Mirage showing encrypts-files, T1486, and user files in Downloads encrypted to .heartbreaker. When detonated on bare-metal Apple Silicon in macOS Mirage , the binary installs a persistent LaunchAgent ( /Users/admin/Library/LaunchAgents/com.network.startup.plist ), drops /Users/admin/Desktop/README.txt , and encrypts user documents in /Users/admin/Downloads/ into Invoice_INV-2026-0842.pdf.heartbreaker and Vendor_Payment_Schedule.xlsx.heartbreaker . This triggers both ENCRYPTS_FILES and T1486 ( Data Encrypted for Impact ). Summary of Verified Public Samples Every sample below is publicly available on VirusTotal and carries verified file-encryption behavioral telemetry across diverse file formats and ransomware families: ) 0 / 75 WindowsSystemUpdate ( .k404 ) Zenbox-verified system_update.pyw encrypting Desktop files to .k404 with 0 static AV hits c920140b725f44c223f33d13fd1f8646a9155d34b4b56a8a2bcd7e762a56c80c high-precision confirmation signal, not an exhaustive recall filter. A missing tag does not mean a sample is benign or lacks ransomware logic. Automated sandbox runs will not emit the tag in several common scenarios: Samples that require command-line arguments or passwords: Affiliates often guard execution with a runtime flag (such as LockBit 3.0 builds that require -pass to decrypt their payload). Sandbox evasion, user-interaction gates, or long sleeps: Samples that exit on VM checks ( DETECT_DEBUG_ENVIRONMENT ), stall past the analysis window ( LONG_SLEEPS ), or wait for specific locales or clicks never reach their encryption loop. Unreachable command-and-control key servers: Families that fetch an encryption key from an offline C2 server before touching local files abort prior to file modification. In sample d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645 (INC Ransom), CAPE Sandbox captures the payload binding user files to Windows I/O Completion Ports (IOCP), rewriting user documents into .INC files, and dropping INC-README.txt across directories.

Figure 3: INC Ransom (d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645) Behavior report showing T1486 user-file encryption and user documents rewritten with the .INC extension.

Similarly, sample 98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e (BlackWizardLock) executes unpacked payload code from dynamically allocated memory, stages temporary .~BLWZ.tmp files, overwrites user documents with .BLWZ extensions (such as bitaddress.pdf.BLWZ and cover-letter-uidev.docx.BLWZ), and presents a full-screen Russian extortion lock screen that directs victims to @seedware on Telegram and threatens to destroy the Master Boot Record (MBR) after five wrong key attempts.

Figure 4: BlackWizardLock (98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e) Behavior report showing encrypts-files, T1486 impact, and user documents encrypted into .BLWZ files.
3. Native Apple Silicon macOS Ransomware: Heartbreaker (Historical macOS Sample Rescanned in macOS Mirage, 16 / 75 AV at Analysis)

While native macOS ransomware is rare in the wild compared to Windows, re-analyzing historical macOS samples validates Apple Silicon coverage. Sample 6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18 (first submitted in May 2025 and rescanned in macOS Mirage) is a self-signed 64-bit ARM64 Mach-O binary detected by 16 out of 75 antivirus engines at the time of analysis.

Figure 5: Native macOS Heartbreaker ransomware (6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18) Behavior report in macOS Mirage showing encrypts-files, T1486, and user files in Downloads encrypted to .heartbreaker.

When detonated on bare-metal Apple Silicon in macOS Mirage, the binary installs a persistent LaunchAgent (/Users/admin/Library/LaunchAgents/com.network.startup.plist), drops /Users/admin/Desktop/README.txt, and encrypts user documents in /Users/admin/Downloads/ into Invoice_INV-2026-0842.pdf.heartbreaker and Vendor_Payment_Schedule.xlsx.heartbreaker. This triggers both ENCRYPTS_FILES and T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact).

Summary of Verified Public Samples

Every sample below is publicly available on VirusTotal and carries verified file-encryption behavioral telemetry across diverse file formats and ransomware families:

What This Signal Does Not Catch

tag:encrypts-files is a high-precision confirmation signal, not an exhaustive recall filter. A missing tag does not mean a sample is benign or lacks ransomware logic. Automated sandbox runs will not emit the tag in several common scenarios:

  • Samples that require command-line arguments or passwords: Affiliates often guard execution with a runtime flag (such as LockBit 3.0 builds that require -pass to decrypt their payload).
  • Sandbox evasion, user-interaction gates, or long sleeps: Samples that exit on VM checks (DETECT_DEBUG_ENVIRONMENT), stall past the analysis window (LONG_SLEEPS), or wait for specific locales or clicks never reach their encryption loop.
  • Unreachable command-and-control key servers: Families that fetch an encryption key from an offline C2 server before touching local files abort prior to file modification.
  • DLLs with custom exported entry points: Standard rundll32 detonation executes DllMain, which misses DLL lockers that require calling a specific named or ordinal export with structured arguments.
  • Network-share-only targets or executable file infectors: Samples configured to encrypt only SMB shares, niche database extensions absent from the VM, or parasitic .exe infectors (such as Virlock and Neshta) do not encrypt user documents on the local profile.
  • Safe ransomware simulators and analysis timeouts: Tools that only encrypt their own newly created test files rather than user documents, as well as samples that time out before reaching their encryption loop, do not trigger the tag.
Practical Security Use Cases & VirusTotal Intelligence Queries

Security teams can use tag:encrypts-files (or behaviour_tags:encrypts_files) immediately across VirusTotal Intelligence Search and the v3 REST API to streamline four common workflows:

  1. Building Clean Ransomware Validation Corpora for EDR and Storage Defense: Endpoint protection engineers, NAS/SAN storage security teams, and purple teams need fresh samples guaranteed to perform real disk-level file encryption when testing ransomware rollback and anomaly-detection sensors. Filter directly on samples verified to encrypt user documents across operating systems and architectures:
    • All confirmed file-encrypting samples: entity:file tag:encrypts-files
    • 64-bit Windows PE encryptors: entity:file tag:encrypts-files type:peexe tag:64bits
    • Archive, script, and non-PE file encryptors: entity:file tag:encrypts-files NOT type:peexe
    • macOS Mach-O encryptors (low in-the-wild volume): entity:file tag:encrypts-files type:macho (note: 20 of the first 55 tagged files match NOT type:peexe, mostly ZIP/RAR archives plus .pyw scripts and DLLs)
  2. Uncovering Evasive or Newly Emerged Ransomware Families: Combine dynamic encryption proof with low static antivirus detection thresholds to catch novel packers, custom Go or Rust lockers, or targeted affiliate builds before broad signature coverage arrives:
    • Low-detection file encryptors (< 10 AV detections): entity:file tag:encrypts-files p:10-
  3. Rapid SOC Triage and Impact Prioritization: During incident response, seeing behaviour_tags:crypto on a suspicious binary only tells an analyst that cryptography libraries were linked or called. Seeing encrypts-files paired with T1486 confirms destructive file-encryption capability immediately, enabling faster containment and backup isolation decisions.
  4. Confidential Detonation in Private Scanning: When triaging sensitive incident samples that cannot be uploaded to the public corpus, you can detonate them in Private Scanning to run the same CAPE, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage checks inside an isolated tenant.
Real-Time Hunting with VirusTotal Livehunt and YARA-X

Beyond retrospective search, you can receive real-time IOC Stream notifications whenever newly submitted or sandbox-analyzed files exhibit verified document encryption by pairing VirusTotal Livehunt with the vt YARA-X module.

1. Core Livehunt Rule: Verified ENCRYPTS_FILES Trait

The rule below matches any file whose sandbox behavior emits vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES. Because CAPE, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage only emit this trait after verifying user-document encryption, ANDing T1486 adds no extra precision:

import "vt"

rule HUNT_Ransomware_EncryptsFiles {
  meta:
    description = "Detects files verified to encrypt user documents in sandbox execution (ENCRYPTS_FILES trait)"
    author = "Google Threat Intelligence"
    date = "2026-11-17"
    reference = "https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/livehunt"

  condition:
    for any trait in vt.behaviour.traits : (
      trait == vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES
    )
}
2. Targeted Variant: Evasive / Low-Detection Ransomware Alerting

To focus your SOC or threat research feed strictly on emerging or lightly detected ransomware payloads (such as the 0/75 system_update.pyw script and 3/75 lkd.exe binary above), add a vt.metadata.analysis_stats.malicious threshold:

import "vt"

rule HUNT_Evasive_Ransomware_LowAV_EncryptsFiles {
  meta:
    description = "Alerts on low-detection files (< 10 AV engines) verified to encrypt user documents in sandboxes"
    author = "Google Threat Intelligence"
    date = "2026-11-17"
    reference = "https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/livehunt"

  condition:
    vt.metadata.analysis_stats.malicious < 10 and
    for any trait in vt.behaviour.traits : (
      trait == vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES
    )
}

Two practical tips when authoring Livehunt behavioral rules:

  • Prefer vt.behaviour.traits over vt.metadata.tags for immediate behavioral matching: Livehunt evaluates dynamic rules as soon as sandbox reports finish (vt.behaviour.traits), so checking vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES matches directly on the normalized sandbox report without waiting for downstream file-tag indexing.
  • When (if ever) to query T1486 in Livehunt: Do not AND T1486 onto ENCRYPTS_FILES rules, because vt.behaviour.mitre_attack_techniques aggregates across every sandbox (including broader Zenbox and third-party mappings) and adds no precision over the trait. Only add a case-insensitive technique.id iequals "T1486" check in separate rules when you want broader T1486 hits from third-party sandboxes that do not emit ENCRYPTS_FILES.
Try It Out and Share Your Feedback

tag:encrypts-files (across CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage) and stricter T1486 gating (in CAPE Sandbox) are live in production for newly scanned and re-analyzed files:

  • Where the tag appears: Check the top file header badges or Behavior > Behavior Tags (attributes.tags and behaviour_traits in the v3 API).
  • Where triggering file paths are recorded: Inspect Signatures and File system actions > Files written in the Behavior tab (or signature_matches[].match_data in /api/v3/files/{sha256}/behaviours) to see the specific affected file paths.
  • Evaluating older cached files: Cached reports from earlier scans keep their historical tags. Click Reanalyze in the VirusTotal web UI to queue dynamic runs on eligible sandboxes that have not yet analyzed that hash (POST /api/v3/files/{id}/analyse in the API refreshes static AV only unless the file is re-uploaded or detonated in Private Scanning).

To explore live matches right now, open VirusTotal Intelligence Search (entity:file tag:encrypts-files) or deploy the YARA rules above in VirusTotal Livehunt. If you spot an interesting sample, edge case, or feature request, please contact us.

Happy hunting!

items.title: KPMG Canada Confirms Cyberattack as Hackers Access Confidential Client Tax Documents
items.summary: KPMG Canada confirmed on November 18 that an unauthorized third party accessed confidential tax documents belonging to some of its clients. The accounting and consulting firm said it acted immediately to contain the cybersecurity breach and secure its systems. It is contacting affected clients directly. KPMG did not disclose when the breach occurred, how many clients were affected, or how many files were accessed. The firm also did not explain how the intruder gained access. Its public statement confirms that documents were accessed, but it does not establish whether the intruder copied them or what details the files contained. KPMG spokesperson Sonja Cloutier-Bosworth told BNNBloomberg that the firm’s monitoring found no sign the affected information was available online or being misused. Technology analyst Carmi Levy cautioned that not finding the data online is not proof that it cannot be shared privately or used later. Securing the affected systems stops further access through the same route if that route has been closed, but it cannot recover copies if any were taken. For affected clients, the most useful detail is what was in their specific files. A document containing a Social Insurance Number or banking details calls for a different response than a file with no sensitive identifiers. KPMG has not publicly confirmed that either type of information was exposed, so clients should ask the firm what its review found rather than assume every affected file carried the same risk. Canada Warned of Fake Help Desk Calls A separate October 28 alert from the Canadian Center for Cyber Security warned that callers were posing as internal IT staff at Canadian organizations, including legal and financial firms. The campaign used phone and Microsoft Teams calls to direct employees to fake sign-in pages. KPMG has not linked its breach to that campaign or said that voice phishing was involved. Cyber Security News has covered fake IT support calls on Microsoft Teams in separate incidents. The practical lesson for employees is to verify unexpected password or account reset requests through a known help desk number or service portal, not through contact details supplied by the caller. The Credit Counseling Society recommends asking which information was exposed and considering a fraud alert on your credit file if sensitive details were involved. It also advises monitoring bank and credit accounts for unfamiliar activity. If a breach notice arrives by email or text, verify it using a KPMG contact you already know before opening attachments or providing personal information. Clients should also watch for messages that use tax details to make a request for payment or account access look genuine. Previous tax-season phishing campaigns in the United States show how scammers imitate tax agencies and preparation firms. In Canada, anyone who spots unusual activity in their tax account should go directly to the Canada Revenue Agency’s fraud and identity theft guidance rather than follow a link in an unexpected message. items.title: 8.8 Million NGINX Services Still Potentially Exposed to Critical NGINX2Root Vulnerability
items.summary: Around 8.8 million NGINX services may still be open to the NGINX2Root flaws. Censys live tracker counts 8,823,450 services that run an affected version and offer HTTP/2. Another 441,489 services that were once exposed have since been patched or have turned HTTP/2 off. NGINX2Root is a set of five memory bugs in NGINX that Xint disclosed on 18 November 2026 . Each bug sits in an NGINX worker process and needs a specific feature to be switched on. Xint says an unauthenticated remote user can use any of them to run commands as that worker. The most serious one is CVE-2026-123007 . It affects every official release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, so the flawed code has existed since HTTP/2 first arrived in 2015. Xint chained it with a separate Linux kernel flaw in the SCTP subsystem to get root, and the chain also broke out of a Docker container. NGINX2Root Vulnerability The Censys advisory says each bug needs a different setup. CVE-2026-123007 needs only HTTP/2. CVE-2026-123633 needs HTTP/2 with a backend proxy. CVE-2026-121810 needs HTTP/3 with a backend proxy. CVE-2026-123634 needs DNS lookups at request time plus subrequests. CVE-2026-113425 needs the mail proxy with auth_http. F5 rates all five 8.1 on CVSS v3.1 and 9.2 on CVSS v4.0. Turning off HTTP/2 blocks only two of the five bugs. Servers with HTTP/3, mail proxy, or runtime DNS setups stay open until they are patched. Censys tracks more than 331 million NGINX web properties. About 103.4 million of them hide their version, so they are hard to judge from the outside. The count of 8,823,450 comes from visible versions plus HTTP/2 support, and the real figure could be higher or lower. Distribution builds can also carry a fix without changing the version number. Xint ran its own check on Shodan data from 10 November. Only 21.1% of 56.7 million NGINX hosts showed a version, and 98.9% of those fell inside the affected range for CVE-2026-123007. Censys ARC built a small cleartext HTTP/2 test. It showed different results on vulnerable 1.31.8 and patched 1.31.9, with a capture of only 5.69 MB. That lets defenders check their patches without sending the 60 to 119 GiB of traffic that Rapid7 reported for its later crash and code execution steps. The files are in the Censys GitHub repository . The team also reproduced use-after-free bugs for CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123634 and CVE-2026-113425. It could not reproduce CVE-2026-121810, and none of the tests ended in code execution. The advisory notes that Wiz showed code execution on a plain static-file server, while Rapid7 published a proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007 only. Censys has not verified the kernel flaw or the full root chain. HTTP/2 control frames are hidden by TLS, so network tools see little unless traffic is decrypted. Censys wrote Suricata rules, and signature 9007015 fired once on the vulnerable capture and never on the patched one. The other rules are experimental. Server logs help more. Xint calls a program started by an NGINX worker the clearest sign of a successful break-in. Repeated worker crashes, heavy inbound traffic on one long connection, and large gaps between received bytes and logged request sizes are weaker hints. Access logs miss the frames this bug uses. NGINX Patch Upgrade NGINX Open Source to 1.30.7 or later on the stable branch , or to 1.31.9 or later on mainline. NGINX Plus users should move to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1. Version numbers can be misleading here, because 1.31.8 is vulnerable while the lower 1.30.7 is fixed. Restart the service after updating, since a reload does not replace the running binary. If you cannot patch yet, turn off HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 where possible and keep the mail proxy away from untrusted users. Then check every other setup that matches the list above. Censys saw no exploitation in the wild as of 18 November, and none of the five CVEs were in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. That only reflects one moment in time. NGINX has been busy this year. Our earlier coverage of an HTTP/2 flaw in NGINX and the HTTP/2 Bomb denial-of-service exploit shows the same protocol under repeated pressure. Xint also notes the advisory list grew from two entries in 2025 to 26 by mid-November, which it links to AI-assisted bug hunting.
